I learn in this letter that Don Pedro of Arragon comes this night / to Messina.
This letter tells me that Don Pedro of Aragon arrives in Messina tonight.
He is very near by this: he was not three leagues off when I left / him.
He's very close by now. He was less than nine miles away when I left him.
How many gentlemen have you lost in this action?
How many gentlemen did you lose in this battle?
But few of any sort, and none of name.
Very few of any rank, and none of any note.
A victory is twice itself when the achiever brings home full numbers. / I find here that Don Pedro hath bestowed much honour on a young / Florentine called Claudio.
A victory is doubled when the winner brings home his whole army. This says Don Pedro has given great honour to a young man from Florence called Claudio.

Much deserved on his part, and equally remembered by Don Pedro. / He hath borne himself beyond the promise of his age, doing in the / figure of a lamb the feats of a lion: he hath indeed better bettered / expectation than you must expect of me to tell you how.

He fully deserved it, and Don Pedro has rewarded him just as fully. He has acted far beyond what you'd expect at his age, doing a lion's deeds while looking like a lamb. He has done even better than people hoped, better than I can expect to describe to you.
He hath an uncle here in Messina will be very much glad of it.
He has an uncle here in Messina who will be very glad to hear it.
I have already delivered him letters, and there appears much joy in / him; even so much that joy could not show itself modest enough without / a badge of bitterness.
I've already given him letters, and he seemed overjoyed; so much so that his joy couldn't stay modest without a sign of grief.
Did he break out into tears?
A kind overflow of kindness. There are no faces truer than those that / are so washed; how much better is it to weep at joy than to joy at / weeping!
A natural overflow of feeling. No faces are more honest than those washed with tears like that. How much better it is to weep for joy than to take joy in someone's weeping!
I pray you, is Signior Mountanto returned from the wars or no?
Please tell me, has Signior Show-off come back from the wars or not?
I know none of that name, lady: there was none such in the army / of any sort.
I know no one of that name, lady. There was nobody like that in the army at any rank.
What is he that you ask for, niece?
Who are you asking about, niece?
My cousin means Signior Benedick of Padua.
My cousin means Signior Benedick of Padua.
O! he is returned, and as pleasant as ever he was.
Oh, he's back, and as witty as ever.

He set up his bills here in Messina and challenged Cupid at the / flight; and my uncle's fool, reading the challenge, subscribed for / Cupid, and challenged him at the bird-bolt. I pray you, how many hath / he killed and eaten in these wars? But how many hath he killed? for, / indeed, I promised to eat all of his killing.

He once put up posters here in Messina challenging Cupid to an archery match; and my uncle's jester read the challenge, signed up on Cupid's behalf, and challenged him with blunt bird-arrows. Tell me, how many has he killed and eaten in these wars? Just how many has he killed? Because I promised to eat everything he killed.
Faith, niece, you tax Signior Benedick too much; but he'll be meet with / you, I doubt it not.
Really, niece, you're too hard on Signior Benedick. But he'll get even with you, I'm sure.
He hath done good service, lady, in these wars.
He has served well in these wars, lady.
You had musty victual, and he hath holp to eat it; he is a very / valiant trencher-man; he hath an excellent stomach.
You had stale food, and he helped to eat it. He's a very brave man with a plate; he has an excellent appetite.
And a good soldier too, lady.
And he's a good soldier too, lady.
And a good soldier to a lady; but what is he to a lord?
A good soldier against a lady, yes. But what is he against a man?
A lord to a lord, a man to a man; stuffed with all honourable / virtues.
A lord to a lord, a man to a man, stuffed with every honourable virtue.
It is so indeed; he is no less than a stuffed man; but for the / stuffing,—well, we are all mortal.
That's right. He's nothing but a stuffed dummy. As for what he's stuffed with, well, we all have our faults.
You must not, sir, mistake my niece. There is a kind of merry war / betwixt Signior Benedick and her; they never meet but there's a / skirmish of wit between them.
Don't misunderstand my niece, sir. There's a sort of playful war between Signior Benedick and her. They never meet without a battle of wits.

Alas! he gets nothing by that. In our last conflict four of his five / wits went halting off, and now is the whole man governed with one! so / that if he have wit enough to keep himself warm, let him bear it for a / difference between himself and his horse; for it is all the wealth / that he hath left to be known a reasonable creature. Who is his / companion now? He hath every month a new sworn brother.

Sadly, he gains nothing by it. In our last fight four of his five wits limped away, and now the whole man is run by just one! So if he has enough wit to keep himself warm, let him keep it as the one thing that tells him apart from his horse; it's all he has left to show he is a thinking creature. Who's his best friend now? He has a new sworn brother every month.
Very easily possible: he wears his faith but as the fashion of his / hat; it ever changes with the next block.
Very easily possible. He wears his loyalty like the style of his hat; it changes with every new fashion.
I see, lady, the gentleman is not in your books.
I can see, lady, the gentleman isn't in your good books.
No; an he were, I would burn my study. But, I pray you, who is his / companion? Is there no young squarer now that will make a voyage with / him to the devil?
No; if he were, I'd burn my library. But tell me, who is his friend? Isn't there some young brawler who'll go to the devil with him?
He is most in the company of the right noble Claudio.
He spends most time with the very noble Claudio.

O Lord, he will hang upon him like a disease: he is sooner caught than / the pestilence, and the taker runs presently mad. God help the noble / Claudio! If he have caught the Benedick, it will cost him a thousand / pound ere a' be cured.

Oh Lord, he'll cling to him like a disease. He's caught faster than the plague, and whoever catches him goes mad at once. God help the noble Claudio! If he's caught the Benedick, it'll cost him a thousand pounds before he's cured.
I will hold friends with you, lady.
I'll make sure to stay on your good side, lady.
You will never run mad, niece.
You'll never go mad over him, niece.
No, not till a hot January.
No, not until we get a hot January.
Good Signior Leonato, you are come to meet your trouble: the fashion / of the world is to avoid cost, and you encounter it.
Good Signior Leonato, you've come out to meet your troubles. Most people try to avoid expense, and you go looking for it.
Never came trouble to my house in the likeness of your Grace, for / trouble being gone, comfort should remain; but when you depart from me, / sorrow abides and happiness takes his leave.
Trouble has never come to my house looking like your Grace. When trouble leaves, comfort should stay; but when you leave me, sorrow stays and happiness goes.
You embrace your charge too willingly. I think this is your daughter.
You take on your burden too gladly. I think this is your daughter.
Her mother hath many times told me so.
Her mother has often told me so.
Were you in doubt, sir, that you asked her?
Were you in doubt, sir, that you had to ask her?
Signior Benedick, no; for then were you a child.
No, Signior Benedick, because you were only a child then.
You have it full, Benedick: we may guess by this what you are, being / a man. Truly the lady fathers herself. Be happy, lady, for you are / like an honourable father.
That's got you, Benedick: we can guess from that what kind of man you are. Seriously, the lady looks just like her father. Be happy, lady, for you resemble an honourable father.
If Signior Leonato be her father, she would not have his head on her / shoulders for all Messina, as like him as she is.
Even if Signior Leonato is her father, she wouldn't want his old grey head on her shoulders for all of Messina, however much she looks like him.
I wonder that you will still be talking, Signior Benedick: nobody / marks you.
I'm amazed you keep on talking, Signior Benedick. Nobody is listening to you.
What! my dear Lady Disdain, are you yet living?
What! My dear Lady Disdain, are you still alive?
Is it possible Disdain should die while she hath such meet food to / feed it as Signior Benedick? Courtesy itself must convert to disdain / if you come in her presence.
How could Disdain die when she has such perfect food to feed on as Signior Benedick? Courtesy herself would turn into disdain if you came near her.
Then is courtesy a turncoat. But it is certain I am loved of all ladies, / only you excepted; and I would I could find in my heart that I had not / a hard heart; for, truly, I love none.
Then courtesy is a traitor. But it's certain that all ladies love me, except you; and I wish I could find it in my heart not to be so hard-hearted, because honestly, I love none of them.

A dear happiness to women: they would else have been troubled with a / pernicious suitor. I thank God and my cold blood, I am of your humour / for that. I had rather hear my dog bark at a crow than a man swear he / loves me.

What luck for women: otherwise they'd be pestered by a dreadful suitor. I thank God and my cold blood that I feel the same as you about that. I'd rather hear my dog bark at a crow than hear a man swear he loves me.
God keep your ladyship still in that mind; so some gentleman or other / shall 'scape a predestinate scratched face.
God keep your ladyship in that frame of mind; then some gentleman or other will escape the scratched face he was fated to get.
Scratching could not make it worse, an 'twere such a face as yours / were.
Scratching couldn't make it any worse, if it were a face like yours.
Well, you are a rare parrot-teacher.
Well, you'd be great at teaching a parrot to talk.
A bird of my tongue is better than a beast of yours.
A bird that talks like me is better than a beast that talks like you.
I would my horse had the speed of your tongue, and so good a / continuer. But keep your way, i' God's name; I have done.
I wish my horse had the speed of your tongue and could keep going as long. But go your way, for God's sake; I've finished.
You always end with a jade's trick: I know you of old.
You always end with a cheap trick, like a horse that stops dead. I know you from before.

That is the sum of all, Leonato: Signior Claudio, and Signior Benedick, / my dear friend Leonato hath invited you all. I tell him we shall stay / here at the least a month, and he heartly prays some occasion may / detain us longer: I dare swear he is no hypocrite, but prays from his / heart.

That's everything, Leonato. Signior Claudio and Signior Benedick, my dear friend Leonato has invited you all. I've told him we'll stay here at least a month, and he sincerely hopes something will keep us longer. I'd swear he's no hypocrite and means it from his heart.
If you swear, my lord, you shall not be forsworn. / [To DON JOHN] / Let me bid you welcome, my lord: being reconciled to the prince your / brother, I owe you all duty.
If you swear it, my lord, you won't be proved a liar. Let me welcome you, my lord. Now that you're reconciled with your brother the prince, I owe you every duty.
I thank you: I am not of many words, but I thank you.
Thank you. I'm a man of few words, but thank you.
Please it your Grace lead on?
Will your Grace lead the way?
Your hand, Leonato; we will go together.
Give me your hand, Leonato; we'll go together.
Benedick, didst thou note the daughter of Signior Leonato?
Benedick, did you notice Signior Leonato's daughter?
I noted her not; but I looked on her.
I didn't notice her, but I did look at her.
Is she not a modest young lady?
Isn't she a modest young lady?
Do you question me, as an honest man should do, for my simple true / judgment; or would you have me speak after my custom, as being a / professed tyrant to their sex?
Are you asking me, as an honest man would, for my plain true opinion? Or do you want me to speak as usual, as a sworn tyrant against women?
No; I pray thee speak in sober judgment.
No, please give me a serious opinion.

Why, i' faith, methinks she's too low for a high praise, too brown / for a fair praise, and too little for a great praise; only this / commendation I can afford her, that were she other than she is, she / were unhandsome, and being no other but as she is, I do not like her.

Well, honestly, I think she's too short for high praise, too dark for fair praise, and too small for great praise. The only compliment I can give her is this: if she were different from how she is, she'd be ugly, and being just as she is, I don't like her.
Thou thinkest I am in sport: I pray thee tell me truly how thou / likest her.
You think I'm joking. Please tell me honestly what you think of her.
Would you buy her, that you enquire after her?
Are you planning to buy her, asking about her like this?
Can the world buy such a jewel?
Could the whole world buy such a jewel?

Yea, and a case to put it into. But speak you this with a sad brow, or / do you play the flouting Jack, to tell us Cupid is a good hare-finder, / and Vulcan a rare carpenter? Come, in what key shall a man take you, / to go in the song?

Yes, and a box to keep it in. But are you saying this with a straight face, or are you playing the mocking joker, telling us that blind Cupid is good at spotting hares and Vulcan the blacksmith is a fine carpenter? Come on, what key are you singing in, so I can join the song?
In mine eye she is the sweetest lady that ever I looked on.
In my eyes she's the sweetest lady I've ever seen.

I can see yet without spectacles and I see no such matter: there's / her cousin an she were not possessed with a fury, exceeds her as much / in beauty as the first of May doth the last of December. But I hope you / have no intent to turn husband, have you?

I can still see without glasses, and I see nothing of the kind. Her cousin, if she weren't possessed by a fury, is as far beyond her in beauty as the first of May is beyond the last of December. But I hope you're not planning to become a husband, are you?
I would scarce trust myself, though I had sworn to the contrary, if Hero / would be my wife.
I'd hardly trust myself, even if I'd sworn the opposite, if Hero would be my wife.

Is't come to this, i' faith? Hath not the world one man but he will wear / his cap with suspicion? Shall I never see a bachelor of threescore / again? Go to, i' faith; an thou wilt needs thrust thy neck into a yoke, / wear the print of it and sigh away Sundays. Look! Don Pedro is returned / to seek you.

Has it come to this, really? Isn't there one man in the world who won't wear his hat worrying it hides a cuckold's horns? Will I never see a sixty-year-old bachelor again? Go on, then; if you must stick your neck into a yoke, wear the mark of it and sigh away your Sundays. Look! Don Pedro has come back for you.
What secret hath held you here, that you followed not to Leonato's?
What secret kept you here, so that you didn't follow us to Leonato's?
I would your Grace would constrain me to tell.
I wish your Grace would force me to tell.
I charge thee on thy allegiance.
I order you to, by your loyalty to me.

You hear, Count Claudio: I can be secret as a dumb man; I would have / you think so; but on my allegiance mark you this, on my allegiance: he / is in love. With who? now that is your Grace's part. Mark how short his / answer is: with Hero, Leonato's short daughter.

You hear that, Count Claudio. I can keep a secret like a mute, and I'd like you to believe that; but on my loyalty, notice this, on my loyalty: he's in love. With whom? That's your Grace's line. See how short his answer is: with Hero, Leonato's short daughter.
If this were so, so were it uttered.
If that were true, that's how he'd tell it.
Like the old tale, my lord: 'it is not so, nor 'twas not so; but indeed, / God forbid it should be so.'
Like the old story, my lord: 'It isn't so, and it wasn't so, and God forbid it should be so.'
If my passion change not shortly. God forbid it should be otherwise.
Unless my feelings change soon, God forbid it should be otherwise.
Amen, if you love her; for the lady is very well worthy.
Amen, if you love her, for she is very worthy.
You speak this to fetch me in, my lord.
You're saying this to trap me, my lord.
By my troth, I speak my thought.
Upon my word, I'm saying what I think.
And in faith, my lord, I spoke mine.
And honestly, my lord, I said what I think.
And by my two faiths and troths, my lord, I spoke mine.
And by both my words of honour, my lord, I said what I think.
That I love her, I feel.
That I love her, I feel.
That she is worthy, I know.
That she is worthy, I know.
That I neither feel how she should be loved nor know how she should / be worthy, is the opinion that fire cannot melt out of me: I will die / in it at the stake.
That I can't feel why she should be loved or know why she's worthy is an opinion that fire couldn't burn out of me. I'll die for it at the stake.
Thou wast ever an obstinate heretic in the despite of beauty.
You were always a stubborn heretic in your contempt for beauty.
And never could maintain his part but in the force of his will.
And he could only keep up his act by sheer stubbornness.

That a woman conceived me, I thank her; that she brought me up, I / likewise give her most humble thanks; but that I will have a recheat / winded in my forehead, or hang my bugle in an invisible baldrick, all / women shall pardon me. Because I will not do them the wrong to / mistrust any, I will do myself the right to trust none; and the fine / is,—for the which I may go the finer,—I will live a bachelor.

I thank a woman for giving birth to me; for bringing me up I humbly thank her too. But I'll never have a hunting horn blown on my forehead or hang my horn in an invisible belt, and all women will have to forgive me. Since I won't insult any woman by distrusting her, I'll do myself the favour of trusting none; and the end of it is (and I'll be the better dressed for it) I'll live a bachelor.
I shall see thee, ere I die, look pale with love.
I'll see you looking pale with love before I die.

With anger, with sickness, or with hunger, my lord; not with love: prove / that ever I lose more blood with love than I will get again with / drinking, pick out mine eyes with a ballad-maker's pen and hang me up at / the door of a brothel-house for the sign of blind Cupid.

Pale with anger, with sickness or with hunger, my lord, but not with love. If you can prove I ever lose more blood through love than I can win back with a drink, then pick out my eyes with a love poet's pen and hang me over the door of a brothel as the sign of blind Cupid.
Well, if ever thou dost fall from this faith, thou wilt prove a notable / argument.
Well, if you ever give up this belief, you'll be a famous example.
If I do, hang me in a bottle like a cat and shoot at me; and he that / hits me, let him be clapped on the shoulder and called Adam.
If I do, hang me in a basket like a cat and shoot arrows at me; and whoever hits me can be slapped on the back and called a champion archer.
Well, as time shall try: 'In time the savage bull doth bear the yoke.'
Well, time will tell. 'In time the wild bull accepts the yoke.'

The savage bull may; but if ever the sensible Benedick bear it, pluck / off the bull's horns and set them in my forehead; and let me be vilely / painted, and in such great letters as they write, 'Here is good horse / to hire,' let them signify under my sign 'Here you may see Benedick / the married man.'

The wild bull may; but if the sensible Benedick ever accepts it, pull off the bull's horns and stick them on my forehead. Then paint me crudely, and in big letters like the ones on signs saying 'Good horse for hire', let them write under my picture: 'Here you may see Benedick the married man.'
If this should ever happen, thou wouldst be horn-mad.
If that ever happened, you'd be raving mad, horns and all.
Nay, if Cupid have not spent all his quiver in Venice, thou wilt quake / for this shortly.
No, if Cupid hasn't used up all his arrows in Venice, you'll soon tremble for this.
I look for an earthquake too then.
Then I'll expect an earthquake too.

Well, you will temporize with the hours. In the meantime, good Signior / Benedick, repair to Leonato's: commend me to him and tell him I will / not fail him at supper; for indeed he hath made great preparation.
Well, you'll soften with time. Meanwhile, good Signior Benedick, go to Leonato's. Give him my regards and tell him I'll be at supper without fail, because he has gone to a lot of trouble over it.
I have almost matter enough in me for such an embassage; and so I / commit you—
I have almost enough sense in me for such an important errand; and so I leave you—
To the tuition of God: from my house, if I had it,—
In the care of God: from my house, if I had one,—
The sixth of July: your loving friend, Benedick.
The sixth of July: your loving friend, Benedick.

Nay, mock not, mock not. The body of your discourse is sometime guarded / with fragments, and the guards are but slightly basted on neither: ere / you flout old ends any further, examine your conscience: and so I leave / you.

No, don't mock me. Your talk is sometimes trimmed with bits and pieces, and even the trimmings are loosely stitched on. Before you poke fun at old phrases any more, check your own conscience. And so I leave you.
My liege, your highness now may do me good.
My lord, your Highness could help me now.
My love is thine to teach: teach it but how, / And thou shalt see how apt it is to learn / hard lesson that may do thee good.
My love is yours to teach. Just show it how, and you'll see how quickly it learns any hard lesson that could do you good.
Hath Leonato any son, my lord?
Does Leonato have a son, my lord?
No child but Hero; she's his only heir. / Dost thou affect her, Claudio?
No child but Hero; she's his only heir. Do you love her, Claudio?

O! my lord, / When you went onward on this ended action, / I looked upon her with a soldier's eye, / That lik'd, but had a rougher task in hand / Than to drive liking to the name of love; / But now I am return'd, and that war-thoughts / Have left their places vacant, in their rooms / Come thronging soft and delicate desires, / All prompting me how fair young Hero is, / Saying, I lik'd her ere I went to wars.

Oh, my lord, when you set off on this war that's now over, I looked at her with a soldier's eye. I liked her, but I had a tougher job in hand than to turn liking into love. But now I'm back, and thoughts of war have left their places empty, and soft, delicate desires come crowding in, all telling me how lovely young Hero is and saying I liked her before I went to war.

Thou wilt be like a lover presently, / And tire the hearer with a book of words. / If thou dost love fair Hero, cherish it, / And I will break with her, and with her father, / And thou shalt have her. Was't not to this end / That thou began'st to twist so fine a story?

You'll soon be just like a lover, and bore your listener with a book of words. If you love beautiful Hero, hold on to it, and I'll speak to her and her father, and you'll have her. Wasn't that why you began to spin such a fine story?
How sweetly you do minister to love, / That know love's grief by his complexion! / But lest my liking might too sudden seem, / I would have salv'd it with a longer treatise.
How sweetly you look after love, recognising love's pain from my face! But in case my feelings seemed too sudden, I wanted to explain them at more length.

What need the bridge much broader than the flood? / The fairest grant is the necessity. / Look, what will serve is fit: 'tis once, thou lov'st, / And I will fit thee with the remedy. / I know we shall have revelling to-night: / I will assume thy part in some disguise, / And tell fair Hero I am Claudio; / And in her bosom I'll unclasp my heart, / And take her hearing prisoner with the force / And strong encounter of my amorous tale: / Then, after to her father will I break; / And the conclusion is, she shall be thine. / In practice let us put it presently.

Why build the bridge any wider than the river? The best gift is what's needed. Look, whatever works is right. In short, you love her, and I'll give you the cure. I know there'll be a party tonight. I'll take your place in a disguise and tell lovely Hero I am Claudio. I'll open my heart to her and take her ears prisoner with the force and power of my loving words. Then I'll speak to her father, and the result will be that she's yours. Let's put it into action right away.
How now, brother! Where is my cousin your son? Hath he provided / this music?
Well, brother! Where's my nephew, your son? Has he arranged this music?
He is very busy about it. But, brother, I can tell you strange / news that you yet dreamt not of.
He's very busy with it. But, brother, I can tell you strange news you never dreamed of.

As the event stamps them: but they have a good cover; they show well / outward. The prince and Count Claudio, walking in a thick-pleached / alley in my orchard, were thus much overheard by a man of mine: the / prince discovered to Claudio that he loved my niece your daughter and / meant to acknowledge it this night in a dance; and if he found her / accordant, he meant to take the present time by the top and instantly / break with you of it.

That depends on how things turn out, but it looks good on the outside. The prince and Count Claudio were walking along a thickly hedged path in my orchard and were overheard by one of my men. The prince told Claudio that he loved my niece, your daughter, and meant to tell her so tonight at the dance; and if she agreed, he meant to seize the moment and speak to you about it at once.
Hath the fellow any wit that told you this?
Has the man who told you this got any sense?
A good sharp fellow: I will send for him; and question him / yourself.
He's a sharp fellow. I'll send for him, and you can question him yourself.

No, no; we will hold it as a dream till it appear itself: but I will / acquaint my daughter withal, that she may be the better prepared for / an answer, if peradventure this be true. Go you, and tell her of it.
No, no. We'll treat it as a dream until it really happens. But I'll tell my daughter about it, so she'll be better prepared with an answer in case it is true. Go and tell her about it.
Cousins, you know what you have to do. O! I cry you mercy, friend; go / you with me, and I will use your skill. Good cousin, have a care this / busy time.
Cousins, you know what you have to do. Oh, I beg your pardon, friend; come with me, and I'll make use of your skill. Good cousin, take care in this busy time.
What the good-year, my lord! why are you thus out of measure sad?
What the devil, my lord! Why are you so terribly gloomy?
There is no measure in the occasion that breeds; therefore the sadness / is without limit.
There's no limit to the thing that causes it, so the gloom has no limit either.
And when I have heard it, what blessings brings it?
And when I've listened, what good does it do me?
If not a present remedy, at least a patient sufferance.
If not an instant cure, at least the patience to bear it.

I wonder that thou, being,—as thou say'st thou art,—born under / Saturn, goest about to apply a moral medicine to a mortifying / mischief. I cannot hide what I am: I must be sad when I have cause, / and smile at no man's jests; eat when I have stomach, and wait for no / man's leisure; sleep when I am drowsy, and tend on no man's business; / laugh when I am merry, and claw no man in his humour.

I'm surprised that you, born under gloomy Saturn as you say you were, try to apply moral medicine to a fatal disease. I can't hide what I am. I must be sad when I have reason, and smile at no one's jokes; eat when I'm hungry and wait for nobody's convenience; sleep when I'm tired and do no one's business; laugh when I'm happy and flatter no one in his moods.

Yea; but you must not make the full show of this till you may do it / without controlment. You have of late stood out against your brother, / and he hath ta'en you newly into his grace; where it is impossible you / should take true root but by the fair weather that you make yourself: / it is needful that you frame the season for your own harvest.

Yes, but you mustn't show all this until you can do it without anyone controlling you. You recently rebelled against your brother, and he has only just taken you back into favour. You can't put down real roots there unless you make the good weather yourself. You need to create the right season for your own harvest.

I had rather be a canker in a hedge than a rose in his grace; and it / better fits my blood to be disdained of all than to fashion a carriage / to rob love from any: in this, though I cannot be said to be a / flattering honest man, it must not be denied but I am a plain-dealing / villain. / I am trusted with a muzzle and enfranchised with a clog; therefore I / have decreed not to sing in my cage. If I had my mouth, I would bite; / if I had my liberty, I would do my liking: in the meantime, let me be / that I am, and seek not to alter me.

I'd rather be a wild rose in a hedge than a cultivated rose in his favour. It suits my nature better to be despised by everyone than to put on an act to steal anyone's love. In this, though no one can call me a flattering honest man, no one can deny I'm a plain, honest villain. I'm trusted only with a muzzle on and freed only with a weight on my leg, so I've decided not to sing in my cage. If I had my mouth free, I would bite; if I had my freedom, I'd do as I like. Meanwhile, let me be what I am, and don't try to change me.
Can you make no use of your discontent?
Can't you make some use of your discontent?
I make all use of it, for I use it only. Who comes here?
I make every use of it, for it's all I use. Who's coming?
I came yonder from a great supper: the prince your brother is royally / entertained by Leonato; and I can give you intelligence of an / intended marriage.
I've come from a great supper over there. The prince your brother is being royally entertained by Leonato, and I can tell you about a planned marriage.
Will it serve for any model to build mischief on? What is he for a / fool that betroths himself to unquietness?
Could it be a foundation to build trouble on? Who's the fool who's promising himself to a lifetime of trouble?
Marry, it is your brother's right hand.
Why, it's your brother's right-hand man.
Who? The ever so perfect Claudio?
A proper squire! And who, and who? which way looks he?
A fine young gentleman! And who is it? Who? Which way is he looking?
Marry, on Hero, the daughter and heir of Leonato.
At Hero, Leonato's daughter and heir.
A very forward March-chick! How came you to this?
A very forward young chick, hatched too early! How did you find this out?

Being entertained for a perfumer, as I was smoking a musty room, comes / me the prince and Claudio, hand in hand, in sad conference: I whipt me / behind the arras, and there heard it agreed upon that the prince should / woo Hero for himself, and having obtained her, give her to Count Claudio.

I'd been hired to perfume the house, and as I was burning herbs in a stuffy room, in came the prince and Claudio arm in arm, deep in serious talk. I slipped behind the tapestry and heard them agree that the prince would woo Hero for himself and, once he'd won her, give her to Count Claudio.

Come, come; let us thither: this may prove food to my displeasure. That / young start-up hath all the glory of my overthrow: if I can cross him / any way, I bless myself every way. You are both sure, and will assist me?

Come on, let's go there. This may feed my anger. That young upstart has all the glory of my defeat. If I can thwart him in any way, I'll count myself lucky in every way. You're both reliable and will help me?
Let us to the great supper: their cheer is the greater that I am / subdued. Would the cook were of my mind! Shall we go to prove what's / to be done?
Let's go to the great supper. Their party is all the merrier because I've been beaten. I wish the cook felt like I do and poisoned them! Shall we go and see what can be done?
Was not Count John here at supper?
Wasn't Count John here at supper?
How tartly that gentleman looks! I never can see him but I am / heart-burned an hour after.
How sour that gentleman looks! I can never see him without getting heartburn for an hour afterwards.
He is of a very melancholy disposition.
He has a very gloomy nature.

He were an excellent man that were made just in the mid-way between / him and Benedick: the one is too like an image, and says nothing; and / the other too like my lady's eldest son, evermore tattling.
The perfect man would be made exactly halfway between him and Benedick. One is too like a statue and says nothing, and the other is too like a spoilt eldest son, forever chattering.
Then half Signior Benedick's tongue in Count John's mouth, and half / Count John's melancholy in Signior Benedick's face,—
Then half of Signior Benedick's tongue in Count John's mouth, and half of Count John's gloom in Signior Benedick's face,—
With a good leg and a good foot, uncle, and money enough in his purse, / such a man would win any woman in the world if a' could get her good / will.
With a good leg and a good foot, uncle, and enough money in his purse, a man like that could win any woman in the world, if he could win her approval.
By my troth, niece, thou wilt never get thee a husband, if thou be / so shrewd of thy tongue.
Honestly, niece, you'll never get yourself a husband if you're so sharp-tongued.
Too curst is more than curst: I shall lessen God's sending that way; / for it is said, 'God sends a curst cow short horns;' but to a cow too / curst he sends none.
Too bad-tempered is more than bad-tempered, so I'll reduce what God sends me that way; for they say 'God sends a bad-tempered cow short horns', but to a cow that's too bad-tempered he sends none.
So, by being too curst, God will send you no horns?
So, by being too bad-tempered, God will send you no horns?

Just, if he send me no husband; for the which blessing I am at him / upon my knees every morning and evening. Lord! I could not endure a / husband with a beard on his face: I had rather lie in the woollen.

Exactly, if he sends me no husband; and I pray to him on my knees for that blessing every morning and evening. Lord! I couldn't stand a husband with a beard on his face. I'd rather sleep in scratchy wool blankets.
You may light on a husband that hath no beard.
You might find a husband who has no beard.

What should I do with him? dress him in my apparel and make him my / waiting-gentlewoman? He that hath a beard is more than a youth, and he / that hath no beard is less than a man; and he that is more than a / youth is not for me; and he that is less than a man, I am not for him: / therefore I will even take sixpence in earnest of the bear-ward, and / lead his apes into hell.

What would I do with him? Dress him in my clothes and make him my lady's maid? A man with a beard is more than a boy, and a man with no beard is less than a man; and the one who's more than a boy isn't for me, and for the one who's less than a man, I'm not for him. So I'll take sixpence in advance from the bear-keeper and lead his apes into hell, the way old maids are supposed to.
Well then, go you into hell?
Well then, will you go to hell?

No; but to the gate; and there will the devil meet me, like an old / cuckold, with horns on his head, and say, 'Get you to heaven, / Beatrice, get you to heaven; here's no place for you maids: 'so / deliver I up my apes, and away to Saint Peter for the heavens; he / shows me where the bachelors sit, and there live we as merry as the / day is long.

No, only to the gate; and there the devil will meet me, like an old cuckold with horns on his head, and say, 'Off you go to heaven, Beatrice, off you go to heaven; there's no place here for you virgins.' So I'll hand over my apes and head off to Saint Peter at the gates of heaven. He'll show me where the bachelors sit, and there we'll live as happily as the day is long.
[To Hero.] Well, niece, I trust you will be ruled by your father.
Well, niece, I trust you'll be guided by your father.

Yes, faith; it is my cousin's duty to make curtsy, and say, / 'Father, as it please you:'— but yet for all that, cousin, let him / be a handsome fellow, or else make another curtsy, and say, / 'Father, as it please me.'

Yes, of course. It's my cousin's duty to curtsy and say, 'Father, as you please.' But all the same, cousin, make sure he's a handsome fellow, or else make another curtsy and say, 'Father, as I please.'
Well, niece, I hope to see you one day fitted with a husband.
Well, niece, I hope to see you one day matched with a husband.

Not till God make men of some other metal than earth. Would it not / grieve a woman to be over-mastered with a piece of valiant dust? to / make an account of her life to a clod of wayward marl? No, uncle, / I'll none: Adam's sons are my brethren; and truly, I hold it a sin / to match in my kinred.

Not until God makes men out of some other material than earth. Wouldn't it upset a woman to be ruled by a lump of swaggering dust? To have to explain her life to a clod of stubborn clay? No, uncle, I won't have one. Adam's sons are my brothers, and I truly think it's a sin to marry a relative.
Daughter, remember what I told you: if the prince do solicit you / in that kind, you know your answer.
Daughter, remember what I told you. If the prince asks you to marry him, you know your answer.

The fault will be in the music, cousin, if you be not wooed in good / time: if the prince be too important, tell him there is measure in / everything, and so dance out the answer. / For, hear me, Hero: wooing, wedding, and repenting is as a Scotch jig, / a measure, and a cinque-pace: the first suit is hot and hasty, like a / Scotch jig, and full as fantastical; the wedding, mannerly-modest, as / a measure, full of state and ancientry; and then comes Repentance, and / with his bad legs, falls into the cinque-pace faster and faster, till / he sink into his grave.

It'll be the music's fault, cousin, if you're not wooed in good time. If the prince is too pushy, tell him there's a proper rhythm to everything, and dance your answer out. Because, listen, Hero: wooing, wedding and regretting are like a Scottish jig, a stately dance and a five-step galliard. The proposal is hot and hasty, like a Scottish jig, and just as wild. The wedding is polite and modest, like a stately dance, all ceremony and tradition. And then along comes Regret, and on his bad legs he stumbles into the galliard, faster and faster, until he sinks into his grave.
Niece, you see things very sharply.
I have a good eye, uncle: I can see a church by daylight.
I have good eyesight, uncle. I can see a church in broad daylight.
The revellers are entering, brother: make good room.
The masked dancers are coming in, brother. Make plenty of room.
Lady, will you walk about with your friend?
Lady, will you walk around with your admirer?
So you walk softly and look sweetly and say nothing, I am yours / for the walk; and especially when I walk away.
As long as you walk slowly, look sweet and say nothing, I'm yours for the walk; especially when I walk away.
I may say so, when I please.
I may say so, when I feel like it.
And when please you to say so?
And when will you feel like saying so?
When I like your favour; for God defend the lute should be like / the case!
When I like your face; for God forbid the lute should look like its case!
My visor is Philemon's roof; within the house is Jove.
My mask is like the roof of Philemon's humble cottage: inside the house is the god Jove.
Why, then, your visor should be thatch'd.
Then your mask should be thatched, like Philemon's roof.
Speak low, if you speak love. / [Takes her aside.]
Speak quietly, if you're speaking of love.
Well, I would you did like me.
Well, I wish you liked me.
So would not I, for your own sake; for I have many ill qualities.
I wouldn't, for your own sake, because I have many bad qualities.
I say my prayers out loud.
I love you the better; the hearers may cry Amen.
I love you all the more for it; the listeners can say Amen.
God match me with a good dancer!
May God pair me with a good dancer!
And God keep him out of my sight when the dance is done! Answer, / clerk.
And may God keep him out of my sight once the dance is over! Your response, parish clerk.
No more words: the clerk is answered.
No more words: the clerk has had his answer.
I know you well enough: you are Signior Antonio.
I know you well enough. You're Signior Antonio.
At a word, I am not.
I know you by the waggling of your head.
I know you by the way your head wobbles.
To tell you true, I counterfeit him.
To tell you the truth, I'm imitating him.
You could never do him so ill-well, unless you were the very man. / Here's his dry hand up and down: you are he, you are he.
You could never copy his faults so perfectly unless you were the man himself. Here's his dry old hand exactly. You're him, you're him.
At a word, I am not.
Come, come; do you think I do not know you by your excellent wit? / Can virtue hide itself? Go to, mum, you are he: graces will appear, / and there's an end.
Come on, do you think I don't recognise you by your excellent wit? Can goodness hide itself? Go on, say nothing, you're him. Good qualities will always show, and that's that.
Will you not tell me who told you so?
Won't you tell me who told you that?
No, you'll have to excuse me.
Nor will you not tell me who you are?
And you won't tell me who you are either?
That I was disdainful, and that I had my good wit out of the / 'Hundred Merry Tales.' Well, this was Signior Benedick that said so.
That I was scornful, and that I got my jokes from a cheap joke book. Well, it was Signior Benedick who said that.
I am sure you know him well enough.
I'm sure you know him well enough.
Did he never make you laugh?
Hasn't he ever made you laugh?
I pray you, what is he?
Please tell me, who is he?

Why, he is the prince's jester: a very dull fool; only his gift is in / devising impossible slanders: none but libertines delight in him; and / the commendation is not in his wit, but in his villany; for he both / pleases men and angers them, and then they laugh at him and beat him. / I am sure he is in the fleet: I would he had boarded me!

Why, he's the prince's jester, a very dull fool. His only talent is inventing unbelievable slanders. Only loose-living men enjoy him, and they like him not for his wit but for his nastiness; for he both pleases men and angers them, so they laugh at him and then beat him. I'm sure he's in the fleet of dancers here. I wish he had sailed up to me!
When I know the gentleman, I'll tell him what you say.
When I meet the gentleman, I'll tell him what you said.

Do, do: he'll but break a comparison or two on me; which, / peradventure not marked or not laughed at, strikes him into melancholy; / and then there's a partridge wing saved, for the fool will eat no / supper that night. / [Music within.] We must follow the leaders.

Do, do. He'll only fire off a comparison or two about me; and if nobody notices or laughs, it'll throw him into a sulk; and then a partridge wing is saved, because the fool won't eat any supper that night. We must follow the leaders.
Nay, if they lead to any ill, I will leave them at the next turning.
No, if they lead to anything bad, I'll leave them at the next turning.
Sure my brother is amorous on Hero, and hath withdrawn her father / to break with him about it. The ladies follow her and but one visor / remains.
My brother is clearly in love with Hero and has taken her father aside to discuss it. The ladies have gone with her, and only one masked man is left.
And that is Claudio: I know him by his bearing.
And that's Claudio. I know him by the way he carries himself.
You know me well; I am he.
You know me well; I am.
Signior, you are very near my brother in his love: he is enamoured / on Hero; I pray you, dissuade him from her; she is no equal for his / birth: you may do the part of an honest man in it.
Signior, you're very close to my brother. He's in love with Hero. Please talk him out of it; she's not his equal in birth. You'd be acting as an honest man in doing it.
How know you he loves her?
How do you know he loves her?
I heard him swear his affection.
I heard him swear his love.
So did I too; and he swore he would marry her to-night.
So did I, and he swore he would marry her tonight.
Come, let us to the banquet.
Come, let's go to the banquet.

Thus answer I in name of Benedick, / But hear these ill news with the ears of Claudio. / 'Tis certain so; the prince wooes for himself. / Friendship is constant in all other things / Save in the office and affairs of love: / herefore all hearts in love use their own tongues; / Let every eye negotiate for itself / And trust no agent; for beauty is a witch / Against whose charms faith melteth into blood. / This is an accident of hourly proof, / Which I mistrusted not. Farewell, therefore, Hero!

I answered like that pretending to be Benedick, but I hear this bad news with Claudio's ears. It's definitely true: the prince is wooing for himself. Friendship is loyal in everything except the business of love. So all lovers should use their own tongues. Let every eye negotiate for itself and trust no go-between; for beauty is a witch whose spells melt loyalty into lust. This happens every hour of the day, and I never suspected it. So goodbye, Hero!
Come, will you go with me?
Come on, will you come with me?

Even to the next willow, about your own business, count. What fashion / will you wear the garland of? About your neck, like a usurer's chain? / or under your arm, like a lieutenant's scarf? You must wear it one way, / for the prince hath got your Hero.

Just to the nearest willow tree, count, on your own business. How will you wear your willow garland of a rejected lover? Round your neck like a moneylender's gold chain? Or under your arm like an officer's sash? You'll have to wear it somehow, because the prince has got your Hero.
I wish him joy of her.
I hope she makes him happy.
Why, that's spoken like an honest drovier: so they sell bullocks. / But did you think the prince would have served you thus?
Why, that's spoken like an honest cattle dealer; that's what they say when they sell bullocks. But did you think the prince would treat you like this?
Ho! now you strike like the blind man: 'twas the boy that stole / your meat, and you'll beat the post.
Ho! Now you're hitting out like the blind man: it was the boy who stole your meat, and you're beating the post.
If it will not be, I'll leave you.
If you won't go, I'll leave you.

Alas! poor hurt fowl. Now will he creep into sedges. But, that my Lady / Beatrice should know me, and not know me! The prince's fool! Ha! it / may be I go under that title because I am merry. Yea, but so I am apt / to do myself wrong; I am not so reputed: it is the base though bitter / disposition of Beatrice that puts the world into her person, and so / gives me out. Well, I'll be revenged as I may.

Poor wounded bird! Now he'll creep off into the reeds. But that my Lady Beatrice should know me and not know me! The prince's fool! Ha! Maybe I'm called that because I'm cheerful. Yes, but I'm being unfair to myself; that's not my reputation. It's Beatrice's low, bitter nature that makes her think she speaks for the whole world, and so she reports me that way. Well, I'll get my revenge however I can.
Now, signior, where's the count? Did you see him?
Now, signior, where's the count? Have you seen him?

Troth, my lord, I have played the part of Lady Fame. I found him here / as melancholy as a lodge in a warren. I told him, and I think I told / him true, that your Grace had got the good will of this young lady; / and I offered him my company to a willow tree, either to make him a / garland, as being forsaken, or to bind him up a rod, as being worthy / to be whipped.

Honestly, my lord, I've played the part of Rumour. I found him here as gloomy as a gamekeeper's lonely hut. I told him, and I think I told him the truth, that your Grace had won this young lady's love. And I offered to take him to a willow tree, either to make him a garland because he's been jilted, or to make him a switch, because he deserves to be whipped.
To be whipped! What's his fault?
To be whipped! What has he done wrong?
The flat transgression of a school-boy, who, being overjoy'd with / finding a bird's nest, shows it his companion, and he steals it.
The plain offence of a schoolboy who's so delighted at finding a bird's nest that he shows it to his friend, and the friend steals it.
Wilt thou make a trust a transgression? The transgression is in / the stealer.
Would you call trusting someone an offence? The offence is the thief's.

Yet it had not been amiss the rod had been made, and the garland too; / for the garland he might have worn himself, and the rod he might have / bestowed on you, who, as I take it, have stolen his bird's nest.
Still, it wouldn't have been wrong to make the switch and the garland too. He could have worn the garland himself and given the switch to you, since, as I see it, you've stolen his bird's nest.
I will but teach them to sing, and restore them to the owner.
I'll only teach the birds to sing and then give them back to their owner.
If their singing answer your saying, by my faith, you say honestly.
If their singing matches your words, then honestly, you're telling the truth.
The Lady Beatrice hath a quarrel to you: the gentleman that danced / with her told her she is much wronged by you.
The Lady Beatrice has a quarrel with you. The gentleman who danced with her told her you've insulted her badly.

O! she misused me past the endurance of a block: an oak but with one / green leaf on it, would have answered her: my very visor began to / assume life and scold with her. / She told me, not thinking I had been myself, that I was the prince's / jester, that I was duller than a great thaw; huddling jest upon jest / with such impossible conveyance upon me, that I stood like a man at a / mark, with a whole army shooting at me. / She speaks poniards, and every word stabs: if her breath were as / terrible as her terminations, there were no living near her; she would / infect to the north star. I would not marry her, though she were / endowed with all that Adam had left him before he transgressed: she / would have made Hercules have turned spit, yea, and have cleft his / club to make the fire too. / Come, talk not of her; you shall find her the infernal Ate in good / apparel. I would to God some scholar would conjure her, for certainly, / while she is here, a man may live as quiet in hell as in a sanctuary; / and people sin upon purpose because they would go thither; so indeed, / all disquiet, horror and perturbation follow her.

Oh, she abused me more than a block of wood could stand! An oak tree with only one green leaf left would have answered her back. Even my mask began to come alive and scold her. Not realising it was me, she told me I was the prince's jester and duller than a muddy thaw, piling joke on joke on me so fast and so unbelievably that I stood like a man at a target with a whole army shooting at me. She speaks daggers, and every word stabs. If her breath were as terrible as her words, nobody could live near her; she'd poison everything as far as the North Star. I wouldn't marry her even if she came with everything Adam owned before he sinned. She'd have made Hercules turn the roasting spit in her kitchen, yes, and split his club for firewood too. Come on, don't talk about her. You'll find she's Ate, the goddess of discord, in fine clothes. I wish to God some scholar would exorcise her; for while she's here, a man could live as peacefully in hell as in a church, and people sin on purpose so as to go there. So really, all trouble, horror and chaos follow her.

Will your Grace command me any service to the world's end? I will go / on the slightest errand now to the Antipodes that you can devise to / send me on; I will fetch you a toothpicker now from the furthest inch / of Asia; bring you the length of Prester John's foot; fetch you a hair / off the Great Cham's beard; do you any embassage to the Pygmies, / rather than hold three words' conference with this harpy. You have no / employment for me?

Has your Grace got any job for me at the end of the world? I'll go on the most trivial errand you can think of to the other side of the globe. I'll fetch you a toothpick from the furthest corner of Asia, bring you the size of the legendary Prester John's foot, fetch you a hair from the Emperor of China's beard, or go as your ambassador to the Pygmies, rather than have a three-word conversation with this monster. You've no task for me?
None, but to desire your good company.
None, except to enjoy your good company.
O God, sir, here's a dish I love not: I cannot endure my Lady Tongue.
Oh God, sir, here's a dish I don't like. I can't stand my Lady Tongue.
Come, lady, come; you have lost the heart of Signior Benedick.
Come, lady, come. You've lost Signior Benedick's heart.

Indeed, my lord, he lent it me awhile; and I gave him use for it, a / double heart for a single one: marry, once before he won it of me with / false dice, therefore your Grace may well say I have lost it.

Well, my lord, he lent it to me for a while, and I paid him interest on it: a double heart for his single one. In fact, he once won it from me with loaded dice, so your Grace may well say I've lost it.
You have put him down, lady, you have put him down.
You've put him down, lady, you've put him down.
So I would not he should do me, my lord, lest I should prove the mother / of fools. I have brought Count Claudio, whom you sent me to seek.
I wouldn't want him to put me down, my lord, in case I became the mother of fools. I've brought Count Claudio, whom you sent me to find.
Why, how now, count! wherefore are you sad?
Well, count! Why are you sad?
The count is neither sad, nor sick, nor merry, nor well; but civil / count, civil as an orange, and something of that jealous complexion.
The count is neither sad, nor ill, nor cheerful, nor well; just civil, as civil as a Seville orange, and with a touch of that jealous yellow colour.

I' faith, lady, I think your blazon to be true; though, I'll be sworn, / if he be so, his conceit is false. Here, Claudio, I have wooed in thy / name, and fair Hero is won; I have broke with her father, and, his good / will obtained; name the day of marriage, and God give thee joy!

Truly, lady, I think your description is accurate; though I swear, if he is jealous, his idea is wrong. Here, Claudio, I've wooed in your name, and lovely Hero is won. I've spoken with her father and got his consent. Name the wedding day, and God give you joy!
Count, take of me my daughter, and with her my fortunes: his / Grace hath made the match, and all grace say Amen to it!
Count, take my daughter from me, and with her my fortune. His Grace has made the match, and may all grace say Amen to it!
Silence is the perfectest herald of joy: I were but little happy, if I / could say how much. Lady, as you are mine, I am yours: I give away myself for / you and dote upon the exchange.
Silence is the best messenger of joy. I'd be only a little happy if I could say how happy I am. Lady, as you are mine, I am yours. I give myself away for you and adore the exchange.
Speak, cousin; or, if you cannot, stop his mouth with a kiss, and let / not him speak neither.
Speak, cousin. Or if you can't, stop his mouth with a kiss, and don't let him speak either.
In faith, lady, you have a merry heart.
Truly, lady, you have a cheerful heart.
Yea, my lord; I thank it, poor fool, it keeps on the windy side of care. / My cousin tells him in his ear that he is in her heart.
Yes, my lord, and I thank it, the poor fool; it keeps upwind of worry. My cousin is whispering in his ear that he's in her heart.
Good Lord, for alliance! Thus goes every one to the world but I, and I / am sunburnt. I may sit in a corner and cry heigh-ho for a husband!
Good Lord, another marriage! So everyone gets married except me, and I'm left out in the sun. I can sit in a corner and sigh, 'Oh dear, I want a husband!'
Lady Beatrice, I will get you one.
Lady Beatrice, I'll get you one.
I would rather have one of your father's getting. Hath your Grace ne'er / a brother like you? Your father got excellent husbands, if a maid could / come by them.
I'd rather have one your father got. Hasn't your Grace got a brother like you? Your father made excellent husbands, if a girl could get one of them.
No, my lord, unless I might have another for working days: your Grace / is too costly to wear every day. But, I beseech your Grace, pardon me; / I was born to speak all mirth and no matter.
No, my lord, unless I could have another one for working days; your Grace is too expensive to wear every day. But, I beg your Grace, forgive me. I was born to speak nothing but jokes and no sense.
Your silence most offends me, and to be merry best becomes you; for out / of question, you were born in a merry hour.
Your silence would offend me most, and being merry suits you best; for there's no doubt you were born at a happy hour.
No, sure, my lord, my mother cried; but then there was a star danced, / and under that was I born. Cousins, God give you joy!
No, surely, my lord, my mother cried; but then a star danced, and I was born under it. Cousins, God give you joy!
Niece, will you look to those things I told you of?
Niece, will you see to those things I told you about?
I cry you mercy, uncle. By your Grace's pardon.
I beg your pardon, uncle. Excuse me, your Grace.
By my troth, a pleasant spirited lady.
Upon my word, a lively, cheerful lady.

There's little of the melancholy element in her, my lord: she is never / sad but when she sleeps; and not ever sad then, for I have heard my / daughter say, she hath often dreamed of unhappiness and waked herself / with laughing.
There's very little sadness in her, my lord. She's only serious when she's asleep, and not always then, because I've heard my daughter say she has often had sad dreams and woken herself up laughing.
She cannot endure to hear tell of a husband.
She can't stand hearing about a husband.
O! by no means: she mocks all her wooers out of suit.
Oh, not at all. She mocks all her suitors until they give up.
She were an excellent wife for Benedick.
She would make Benedick an excellent wife.
O Lord! my lord, if they were but a week married, they would talk / themselves mad.
Oh Lord, my lord, if they were married just a week they'd talk each other mad.
Count Claudio, when mean you to go to church?
Count Claudio, when do you plan to go to church?
To-morrow, my lord. Time goes on crutches till love have all his rites.
Tomorrow, my lord. Time walks on crutches until love has had all its ceremonies.
Not till Monday, my dear son, which is hence a just seven-night; and a / time too brief too, to have all things answer my mind.
Not until Monday, my dear son, which is exactly a week from now; and even that's too short a time to get everything as I want it.

Come, you shake the head at so long a breathing; but, I warrant thee, / Claudio, the time shall not go dully by us. I will in the interim / undertake one of Hercules' labours, which is, to bring Signior / Benedick and the Lady Beatrice into a mountain of affection the one / with the other. / I would fain have it a match; and I doubt not but to fashion it, if / you three will but minister such assistance as I shall give you / direction.

Come, you shake your head at such a long wait, but I promise you, Claudio, the time won't pass slowly for us. Meanwhile I'll take on one of the labours of Hercules: to bring Signior Benedick and the Lady Beatrice into a mountain of love for each other. I'd love to make it a match, and I'm sure I can arrange it, if you three will give whatever help I direct.
My lord, I am for you, though it cost me ten nights' watchings.
My lord, I'm with you, even if it costs me ten sleepless nights.
And so am I, my lord.
I will do any modest office, my lord, to help my cousin to a good / husband.
I'll do anything proper, my lord, to help my cousin to a good husband.

And Benedick is not the unhopefullest husband that I know. Thus far / can I praise him; he is of a noble strain, of approved valour, and / confirmed honesty. / I will teach you how to humour your cousin, that she shall fall in / love with Benedick; and I, with your two helps, will so practise on / Benedick that, in despite of his quick wit and his queasy stomach, he / shall fall in love with Beatrice. If we can do this, Cupid is no / longer an archer: his glory shall be ours, for we are the only / love-gods. Go in with me, and I will tell you my drift.

And Benedick is not the most hopeless husband I know. I can praise him this far: he's of noble family, of proven courage and of tested honesty. I'll teach you how to handle your cousin so that she falls in love with Benedick; and I, with the help of you two, will work on Benedick so that, despite his quick wit and his weak stomach for marriage, he'll fall in love with Beatrice. If we can do this, Cupid is no longer the archer. His glory will be ours, for we'll be the only gods of love. Come in with me, and I'll tell you my plan.
It is so; the Count Claudio shall marry the daughter of Leonato.
So it's true. Count Claudio will marry Leonato's daughter.
Yea, my lord; but I can cross it.
Yes, my lord, but I can block it.

Any bar, any cross, any impediment will be medicinable to me: I am / sick in displeasure to him, and whatsoever comes athwart his affection / ranges evenly with mine. How canst thou cross this marriage?
Any barrier, any block, any obstacle will be medicine to me. I'm sick with hatred for him, and whatever cuts across his desires suits mine exactly. How can you block this marriage?
Not honestly, my lord; but so covertly that no dishonesty shall appear / in me.
Not honestly, my lord, but so secretly that I won't seem dishonest at all.
I think I told your lordship, a year since, how much I am in the / favour of Margaret, the waiting-gentlewoman to Hero.
I think I told your lordship a year ago how much Margaret, Hero's lady's maid, likes me.
I can, at any unseasonable instant of the night, appoint her to look / out at her lady's chamber window.
I can arrange for her, at any unlikely hour of the night, to look out of her lady's bedroom window.
What life is in that, to be the death of this marriage?
What life is there in that, to be the death of this marriage?

The poison of that lies in you to temper. Go you to the prince your / brother; spare not to tell him, that he hath wronged his honour in / marrying the renowned Claudio,—whose estimation do you mightily hold / up,—to a contaminated stale, such a one as Hero.

It's up to you to mix the poison. Go to the prince your brother. Don't hold back from telling him that he has damaged his honour by marrying the famous Claudio, whom you must praise to the skies, to a filthy whore like Hero.
What proof shall I make of that?
What proof will I give of that?
Proof enough to misuse the prince, to vex Claudio, to undo Hero, / and kill Leonato. Look you for any other issue?
Proof enough to deceive the prince, torment Claudio, ruin Hero and kill Leonato. Do you want any other outcome?
Only to despite them, I will endeavour anything.
Just to spite them, I'll try anything.

Go then; find me a meet hour to draw Don Pedro and the Count Claudio / alone: tell them that you know that Hero loves me; intend a kind of / zeal both to the prince and Claudio, as—in love of your brother's / honour, who hath made this match, and his friend's reputation, who is / thus like to be cozened with the semblance of a maid,—that you have / discovered thus. / They will scarcely believe this without trial: offer them instances, / which shall bear no less likelihood than to see me at her / chamber-window, hear me call Margaret Hero, hear Margaret term me / Claudio; and bring them to see this the very night before the intended / wedding: for in the meantime I will so fashion the matter that Hero / shall be absent; and there shall appear such seeming truth of Hero's / disloyalty, that jealousy shall be called assurance, and all the / preparation overthrown.

Go then. Find me a suitable time to get Don Pedro and Count Claudio alone. Tell them you know that Hero loves me. Pretend to be full of concern for both the prince and Claudio, as if, out of love for your brother's honour, since he made this match, and for his friend's reputation, since he's about to be cheated with something that only looks like a virgin, you've found this out. They'll hardly believe it without proof. Offer them evidence, no less convincing than seeing me at her bedroom window, hearing me call Margaret 'Hero' and hearing Margaret call me 'Claudio'. Bring them to see this on the very night before the wedding. In the meantime I'll arrange things so that Hero is away, and there'll be such convincing evidence of Hero's unfaithfulness that suspicion will be taken for certainty, and all the wedding plans overturned.
Grow this to what adverse issue it can, I will put it in practice. / Be cunning in the working this, and thy fee is a thousand ducats.
However badly this turns out, I'll put it into action. Be clever in carrying it out, and your fee is a thousand ducats.
Be you constant in the accusation, and my cunning shall not shame me.
You stick firmly to the accusation, and my cleverness won't let me down.
I will presently go learn their day of marriage.
I'll go straight away and find out their wedding day.
In my chamber-window lies a book; bring it hither to me in the / orchard.
There's a book on my bedroom windowsill. Bring it here to me in the orchard.
I know that; but I would have thee hence, and here again.
I know that, but I want you to go away and come back here again.

I do much wonder that one man, seeing how much another man is a fool / when he dedicates his behaviours to love, will, after he hath laughed / at such shallow follies in others, become the argument of his own / scorn by falling in love: and such a man is Claudio. / I have known, when there was no music with him but the drum and the / fife; and now had he rather hear the tabor and the pipe: I have known / when he would have walked ten mile afoot to see a good armour; and now / will he lie ten nights awake, carving the fashion of a new doublet. / He was wont to speak plain and to the purpose, like an honest man and / a soldier; and now is he turned orthography; his words are a very / fantastical banquet, just so many strange dishes. May I be so / converted, and see with these eyes? / I cannot tell; I think not: I will not be sworn but love may transform / me to an oyster; but I'll take my oath on it, till he have made an / oyster of me, he shall never make me such a fool. One woman is fair, / yet I am well; another is wise, yet I am well; another virtuous, yet I / am well; but till all graces be in one woman, one woman shall not come / in my grace. / Rich she shall be, that's certain; wise, or I'll none; virtuous, or / I'll never cheapen her; fair, or I'll never look on her; mild, or come / not near me; noble, or not I for an angel; of good discourse, an / excellent musician, and her hair shall be of what colour it please / God. Ha! the prince and Monsieur Love! I will hide me in the arbour.

It amazes me that one man, seeing what a fool another man is when he devotes himself to love, will laugh at such silly behaviour in others and then become the object of his own scorn by falling in love. And Claudio is just such a man. I've known a time when the only music he liked was the military drum and fife; now he'd rather hear the little drum and pipe of a village dance. I've known a time when he'd have walked ten miles to see a good suit of armour; now he'll lie awake ten nights designing the style of a new jacket. He used to speak plainly and to the point, like an honest man and a soldier; now he's turned into a dictionary. His words are a very fancy banquet, so many exotic dishes. Could I ever be changed like that and see with these same eyes? I can't say; I don't think so. I won't swear that love couldn't turn me into an oyster; but I'll swear this: until he's made an oyster of me, he'll never make such a fool of me. One woman is beautiful, yet I'm fine; another is clever, yet I'm fine; another is good, yet I'm fine. But until all the virtues are in one woman, no woman will win my favour. She'll be rich, that's certain; clever, or I won't have her; good, or I won't even bargain for her; beautiful, or I won't look at her; gentle, or she'd better not come near me; noble, or I wouldn't take her for a gold coin; a good talker, an excellent musician, and her hair can be whatever colour God likes. Ha! The prince and Monsieur Love! I'll hide in the arbour.
Come, shall we hear this music?
Come, shall we listen to this music?
Yea, my good lord. / How still the evening is, / As hush'd on purpose to grace harmony!
Yes, my good lord. How still the evening is, as if it were hushed on purpose to show off the music!
See you where Benedick hath hid himself?
Do you see where Benedick has hidden himself?
O! very well, my lord: the music ended, / We'll fit the kid-fox with a penny-worth.
Oh, very well, my lord. When the music's over, we'll give this sly young fox more than he bargained for.
Come, Balthazar, we'll hear that song again.
Come, Balthazar, let's hear that song again.
O! good my lord, tax not so bad a voice / To slander music any more than once.
Oh, my good lord, don't make such a bad voice insult music more than once.
It is the witness still of excellency, / To put a strange face on his own perfection. / I pray thee, sing, and let me woo no more.
It's always the sign of real excellence to pretend not to recognise its own perfection. Please sing, and don't make me woo you any longer.
Because you talk of wooing, I will sing; / Since many a wooer doth commence his suit / To her he thinks not worthy; yet he wooes; / Yet will he swear he loves.
Since you talk of wooing, I'll sing; for many a wooer starts courting a woman he doesn't think worthy, and yet he woos; and yet he'll swear he loves her.
Nay, pray thee come; / Or if thou wilt hold longer argument, / Do it in notes.
No, please, come on; or if you want to keep arguing, do it in musical notes.
Note this before my notes; / There's not a note of mine that's worth the noting.
Note this before my notes: there's not a note of mine worth noting.
Why these are very crotchets that he speaks; / Notes, notes, forsooth, and nothing!
Why, he's talking in crotchets: quarter notes and quirks! Notes, notes, indeed, and nothing!
Now, divine air! now is his soul ravished! Is it not strange that / sheep's guts should hale souls out of men's bodies? Well, a horn for / my money, when all's done.
Now, heavenly music! Now his soul is carried away! Isn't it strange that sheep's guts strung on a lute can drag souls out of men's bodies? Well, give me a hunting horn, when all's said and done.

Sigh no more, ladies, sigh no more, / Men were deceivers ever; / One foot in sea, and one on shore, / To one thing constant never. / Then sigh not so, / But let them go, / And be you blithe and bonny, / Converting all your sounds of woe / Into Hey nonny, nonny. / Sing no more ditties, sing no mo / Of dumps so dull and heavy; / The fraud of men was ever so, / Since summer first was leavy. / Then sigh not so, / But let them go, / And be you blithe and bonny, / Converting all your sounds of woe / Into Hey nonny, nonny.

Sigh no more, ladies, sigh no more; men were always deceivers. With one foot in the sea and one on the shore, they're never faithful to one thing. So don't sigh like that, but let them go, and be happy and pretty, turning all your sounds of sadness into 'Hey nonny, nonny.' Sing no more songs, sing no more, of gloomy, heavy moods. Men have always cheated like this, ever since the first summer had leaves. So don't sigh like that, but let them go, and be happy and pretty, turning all your sounds of sadness into 'Hey nonny, nonny.'
By my troth, a good song.
Upon my word, a good song.
And an ill singer, my lord.
And a bad singer, my lord.
Ha, no, no, faith; thou singest well enough for a shift.
Ha, no, no, really. You sing well enough when needed.

[Aside.] An he had been a dog that should have howled thus, they would / have hanged him; and I pray God his bad voice bode no mischief. I had / as lief have heard the night-raven, come what plague could have come / after it.
If a dog had howled like that, they'd have hanged it; and I pray to God his bad voice isn't an omen of trouble. I'd rather have heard the night-raven, whatever plague might have followed it.
Yea, marry; dost thou hear, Balthazar? I pray thee, get us some / excellent music, for to-morrow night we would have it at the Lady / Hero's chamber-window.
Yes, indeed. Are you listening, Balthazar? Please get us some excellent music, because tomorrow night we want to play it under the Lady Hero's bedroom window.
The best I can, my lord.
The best I can, my lord.
Come hither, Leonato: what was it you told me of to-day, that your / niece Beatrice was in love with Signior Benedick?
Come here, Leonato. What was it you told me about today, that your niece Beatrice is in love with Signior Benedick?
O! ay:— / [Aside to DON PEDRO] Stalk on, stalk on; the fowl sits. I did never / think that lady would have loved any man.
Oh yes. Keep stalking, keep stalking; the bird has settled. I never thought that lady would love any man.
No, nor I neither; but most wonderful that she should so dote on / Signior Benedick, whom she hath in all outward behaviours seemed ever / to abhor.
No, nor did I. But the most amazing thing is that she should be so infatuated with Signior Benedick, whom she has always seemed to loathe, judging by her behaviour.
[Aside.] Is't possible? Sits the wind in that corner?
Is it possible? Is that the way the wind is blowing?
By my troth, my lord, I cannot tell what to think of it but that she / loves him with an enraged affection: it is past the infinite of thought.
Honestly, my lord, I don't know what to think, except that she loves him with a wild passion. It's beyond all imagining.
May be she doth but counterfeit.
O God! counterfeit! There was never counterfeit of passion came so near / the life of passion as she discovers it.
Oh God, pretending! No pretended passion ever came as close to real passion as hers does.
Why, what effects of passion shows she?
Why, what signs of passion does she show?
[Aside.] Bait the hook well: this fish will bite.
Bait the hook well; this fish will bite.
What effects, my lord? She will sit you; [To Claudio.] You heard / my daughter tell you how.
What signs, my lord? She'll sit there, you heard my daughter tell you how.
How, how, I pray you? You amaze me: I would have thought her spirit / had been invincible against all assaults of affection.
How, how, please tell me? You amaze me. I'd have thought her spirit was invincible against every attack of love.
I would have sworn it had, my lord; especially against Benedick.
I'd have sworn it was, my lord, especially against Benedick.
[Aside] I should think this a gull, but that the white-bearded / fellow speaks it: knavery cannot, sure, hide itself in such reverence.
I'd think this was a trick, except that the white-bearded old man is saying it. Surely villainy can't hide behind someone so respectable.
[Aside.] He hath ta'en the infection: hold it up.
He's caught the infection. Keep it up.
Hath she made her affection known to Benedick?
Has she told Benedick about her love?
No; and swears she never will: that's her torment.
No, and she swears she never will. That's her torment.
Tis true, indeed; so your daughter says: 'Shall I,' says she, 'that / have so oft encountered him with scorn, write to him that I love him?'
It's true, indeed; that's what your daughter says. 'Shall I,' she says, 'who have so often met him with scorn, write to him that I love him?'
This says she now when she is beginning to write to him; for she'll / be up twenty times a night, and there will she sit in her smock till / she have writ a sheet of paper: my daughter tells us all.

That's what she says now, when she's starting to write to him. She'll get up twenty times a night and sit there in her nightdress until she's written a whole sheet of paper. My daughter tells us everything.
Now you talk of a sheet of paper, I remember a pretty jest your / daughter told us of.
Now that you talk of a sheet of paper, I remember a funny joke your daughter told us.
O! when she had writ it, and was reading it over, she found / Benedick and Beatrice between the sheet?
Oh, when she'd written it and was reading it over, she found 'Benedick' and 'Beatrice' lying together between the sheet?

O! she tore the letter into a thousand halfpence; railed at herself, / that she should be so immodest to write to one that she knew would / flout her: 'I measure him,' says she, 'by my own spirit; for I should / flout him, if he writ to me; yea, though I love him, I should.'

Oh, she tore the letter into a thousand tiny pieces and scolded herself for being so shameless as to write to someone she knew would mock her. 'I judge him,' she says, 'by my own spirit; because I would mock him if he wrote to me; yes, even though I love him, I would.'
Then down upon her knees she falls, weeps, sobs, beats her heart, tears / her hair, prays, curses; 'O sweet Benedick! God give me patience!'
Then down she falls on her knees, weeps, sobs, beats her breast, tears her hair, prays and curses: 'Oh sweet Benedick! God give me patience!'
She doth indeed; my daughter says so; and the ecstasy hath so much / overborne her, that my daughter is sometimes afeard she will do a / desperate outrage to herself. It is very true.
She does indeed, my daughter says so. And the frenzy has overcome her so much that my daughter is sometimes afraid she'll do something desperate to herself. It's quite true.
It were good that Benedick knew of it by some other, if she will / not discover it.
It would be good if Benedick heard about it from someone else, if she won't reveal it.
To what end? he would make but a sport of it and torment the poor / lady worse.
What for? He'd only make fun of it and torment the poor lady even more.
An he should, it were an alms to hang him. She's an excellent sweet / lady, and, out of all suspicion, she is virtuous.
If he did, it would be a good deed to hang him. She's an excellent, sweet lady and, beyond all suspicion, virtuous.
In everything but in loving Benedick.
O! my lord, wisdom and blood combating in so tender a body, we have / ten proofs to one that blood hath the victory. I am sorry for her, as / I have just cause, being her uncle and her guardian.
Oh, my lord, when reason and passion fight in such a young body, the odds are ten to one that passion wins. I'm sorry for her, as I've every reason to be, being her uncle and guardian.
