I would she had bestowed this dotage on me; I would have daffed all / other respects and made her half myself. I pray you, tell Benedick of / it, and hear what a' will say.
I wish she'd lavished this adoration on me. I'd have brushed aside every other consideration and made her my wife. Please tell Benedick about it, and hear what he says.
Do you think that would be good?

Hero thinks surely she will die; for she says she will die if he love / her not, and she will die ere she make her love known, and she will die / if he woo her, rather than she will bate one breath of her accustomed / crossness.

Hero is sure she'll die. She says she'll die if he doesn't love her, and she'll die before she reveals her love, and she'll die if he woos her rather than give up one breath of her usual contrariness.
She doth well: if she should make tender of her love, 'tis very / possible he'll scorn it; for the man,—as you know all,—hath a / contemptible spirit.
She's right. If she offered him her love, it's very likely he'd scorn it; for the man, as you all know, has a scornful nature.
He is a very proper man.
He hath indeed a good outward happiness.
He does indeed have good looks.
Fore God, and in my mind, very wise.
By God, and in my opinion, very clever.
He doth indeed show some sparks that are like wit.
He does indeed show some sparks that look like wit.
And I take him to be valiant.
As Hector, I assure you: and in the managing of quarrels you may say / he is wise; for either he avoids them with great discretion, or / undertakes them with a most Christian-like fear.
As brave as Hector, I promise you. And in handling quarrels you could say he's wise, because either he avoids them very sensibly, or he takes them on with a most Christian fear.
If he do fear God, a' must necessarily keep peace: if he break the / peace, he ought to enter into a quarrel with fear and trembling.
If he fears God, he must keep the peace. If he breaks the peace, he ought to start a quarrel with fear and trembling.
And so will he do; for the man doth fear God, howsoever it seems not / in him by some large jests he will make. Well, I am sorry for your / niece. Shall we go seek Benedick and tell him of her love?
And so he will, because the man does fear God, even if it doesn't seem so from some of his crude jokes. Well, I'm sorry for your niece. Shall we go and find Benedick and tell him about her love?
Never tell him, my lord: let her wear it out with good counsel.
Never tell him, my lord. Let her get over it with good advice.
Nay, that's impossible: she may wear her heart out first.
No, that's impossible. She may wear out her heart first.
Well, we will hear further of it by your daughter: let it cool the / while. I love Benedick well, and I could wish he would modestly / examine himself, to see how much he is unworthy so good a lady.
Well, we'll hear more about it from your daughter. Let it cool for now. I'm very fond of Benedick, and I wish he'd take a humble look at himself and see how unworthy he is of such a good lady.
My lord, will you walk? dinner is ready.
My lord, shall we go? Dinner is ready.
[Aside.] If he do not dote on her upon this, I will never trust my / expectation.
If he doesn't adore her after this, I'll never trust my judgment again.

[Aside.] Let there be the same net spread for her; and that must your / daughter and her gentle-woman carry. The sport will be, when they hold / one an opinion of another's dotage, and no such matter: that's the / scene that I would see, which will be merely a dumb-show. Let us send / her to call him in to dinner.

Let the same net be spread for her, and your daughter and her maid must handle that. The fun will be when each one believes the other is madly in love, and there's nothing in it. That's the scene I'd like to see, and it will be pure mime, since neither will dare to speak. Let's send her to call him in to dinner.

[Advancing from the arbour.] This can be no trick: the conference was / sadly borne. They have the truth of this from Hero. They seem to pity / the lady: it seems her affections have their full bent. Love me! why, / it must be requited. / I hear how I am censured: they say I will bear myself proudly, if I / perceive the love come from her; they say too that she will rather die / than give any sign of affection. I did never think to marry: I must / not seem proud: happy are they that hear their detractions, and can / put them to mending. / They say the lady is fair: 'tis a truth, I can bear them witness; and / virtuous: 'tis so, I cannot reprove it; and wise, but for loving me: / by my troth, it is no addition to her wit, nor no great argument of / her folly, for I will be horribly in love with her. / I may chance have some odd quirks and remnants of wit broken on me, / because I have railed so long against marriage; but doth not the / appetite alter? A man loves the meat in his youth that he cannot / endure in his age. / Shall quips and sentences and these paper bullets of the brain awe a / man from the career of his humour? No; the world must be peopled. When / I said I would die a bachelor, I did not think I should live till I / were married. Here comes Beatrice. By this day! she's a fair lady: I / do spy some marks of love in her.

This can't be a trick. They talked seriously. They have the truth of it from Hero. They seem to pity the lady. It seems her love is stretched to the limit. Love me! Why, it must be returned. I hear how I'm criticised. They say I'll be proud if I realise the love comes from her. They also say she would rather die than show any sign of love. I never thought I'd marry. I mustn't seem proud. Happy are those who hear their faults and can correct them. They say the lady is beautiful; that's true, I can vouch for it. And good; that's so, I can't deny it. And clever, except for loving me. Honestly, that doesn't add to her cleverness, but it's no great proof of her foolishness either, because I'm going to be terribly in love with her. Some odd jokes and scraps of wit may be cracked at my expense, because I've attacked marriage for so long. But don't tastes change? A man loves food in his youth that he can't stand in old age. Shall clever remarks and sayings and these paper bullets of the brain scare a man off following his desires? No, the world must be populated. When I said I'd die a bachelor, I didn't think I'd live until I got married. Here comes Beatrice. By heaven! She's a beautiful lady. I do see some signs of love in her.
Against my will I am sent to bid you come in to dinner.
Against my will I've been sent to tell you to come in to dinner.
Fair Beatrice, I thank you for your pains.
Lovely Beatrice, thank you for your trouble.
I took no more pains for those thanks than you take pains to thank me: / if it had been painful, I would not have come.
I took no more trouble earning those thanks than you take to thank me. If it had been any trouble, I wouldn't have come.
You take pleasure then in the message?
So you enjoy bringing the message?
Yea, just so much as you may take upon a knife's point, and choke / a daw withal. You have no stomach, signior: fare you well.
Yes, about as much as you could balance on a knife's point and choke a jackdaw with. You have no appetite, signior. Goodbye.

Ha! 'Against my will I am sent to bid you come in to dinner,' there's / a double meaning in that. 'I took no more pains for those thanks than / you took pains to thank me,' that's as much as to say, Any pains that / I take for you is as easy as thanks. If I do not take pity of her, I / am a villain; if I do not love her, I am a Jew. I will go get her / picture.

Ha! 'Against my will I've been sent to tell you to come in to dinner.' There's a double meaning in that. 'I took no more trouble earning those thanks than you took to thank me.' That's as good as saying, 'Any trouble I take for you is as easy as saying thanks.' If I don't take pity on her, I'm a villain; if I don't love her, I'm a heartless unbeliever. I'll go and get her portrait.

Good Margaret, run thee to the parlour; / There shalt thou find my cousin Beatrice / Proposing with the prince and Claudio: / Whisper her ear, and tell her, I and Ursala / Walk in the orchard, and our whole discourse / Is all of her; say that thou overheard'st us, / And bid her steal into the pleached bower, / Where honey-suckles, ripen'd by the sun, / Forbid the sun to enter; like favourites, / Made proud by princes, that advance their pride / Against that power that bred it. There will she hide her, / To listen our propose. This is thy office; / Bear thee well in it and leave us alone.

Good Margaret, run to the drawing room. You'll find my cousin Beatrice there talking with the prince and Claudio. Whisper in her ear and tell her that Ursula and I are walking in the orchard and that all our talk is about her. Say you overheard us, and tell her to slip into the arbour of woven branches, where honeysuckle, ripened by the sun, won't let the sun come in, like royal favourites who are made proud by princes and then turn their pride against the very power that raised them. She'll hide there to listen to our conversation. This is your job; do it well and leave us alone.
I'll make her come, I warrant you, presently.
I'll make her come right away, I promise you.

Now, Ursula, when Beatrice doth come, / As we do trace this alley up and down, / Our talk must only be of Benedick: / When I do name him, let it be thy part / To praise him more than ever man did merit. / My talk to thee must be how Benedick / Is sick in love with Beatrice: of this matter / Is little Cupid's crafty arrow made, / That only wounds by hearsay.

Now, Ursula, when Beatrice comes, as we walk up and down this path, we must talk only about Benedick. Whenever I mention him, your job is to praise him more than any man ever deserved. What I'll tell you is how Benedick is lovesick for Beatrice. That's what little Cupid's crafty arrow is made of, the kind that wounds just by hearsay.
Now begin; / For look where Beatrice, like a lapwing, runs / Close by the ground, to hear our conference.
Now, begin; for look where Beatrice is running close to the ground like a lapwing, to hear what we say.

The pleasant'st angling is to see the fish / Cut with her golden oars the silver stream, / And greedily devour the treacherous bait: / So angle we for Beatrice; who even now / Is couched in the woodbine coverture. / Fear you not my part of the dialogue.

The most pleasant kind of fishing is watching the fish cut through the silver stream with its golden fins and greedily swallow the treacherous bait. That's how we'll fish for Beatrice, who is already hiding under the honeysuckle. Don't worry about my part of the conversation.
Then go we near her, that her ear lose nothing / Of the false sweet bait that we lay for it.
Then let's go nearer to her, so her ear doesn't miss any of the false sweet bait we're putting out for it.
No, truly, Ursula, she is too disdainful; / I know her spirits are as coy and wild / As haggards of the rock.
No, honestly, Ursula, she's too scornful. I know her spirit is as shy and wild as an untamed hawk from the cliffs.
But are you sure / That Benedick loves Beatrice so entirely?
But are you sure that Benedick loves Beatrice so completely?
So says the prince, and my new-trothed lord.
So says the prince, and my newly engaged lord.
And did they bid you tell her of it, madam?
And did they ask you to tell her about it, madam?
They did entreat me to acquaint her of it; / But I persuaded them, if they lov'd Benedick, / To wish him wrestle with affection, / And never to let Beatrice know of it.
They begged me to let her know; but I persuaded them, if they loved Benedick, to want him to wrestle with his love and never let Beatrice know about it.
Why did you so? Doth not the gentleman / Deserve as full as fortunate a bed / As ever Beatrice shall couch upon?
Why did you do that? Doesn't the gentleman deserve as rich and happy a marriage bed as Beatrice could ever lie in?

O god of love! I know he doth deserve / As much as may be yielded to a man; / But nature never fram'd a woman's heart / Of prouder stuff than that of Beatrice; / Disdain and scorn ride sparkling in her eyes, / Misprising what they look on, and her wit / Values itself so highly, that to her / All matter else seems weak. She cannot love, / Nor take no shape nor project of affection, / She is so self-endear'd.

Oh god of love! I know he deserves as much as any man could be given. But nature never made a woman's heart out of prouder stuff than Beatrice's. Disdain and scorn sparkle in her eyes, despising everything they look at, and she values her own wit so highly that everything else seems feeble to her. She cannot love, or even imagine what love looks like; she's so in love with herself.
Sure I think so; And therefore certainly it were not good / She knew his love, lest she make sport at it.
I'm sure you're right. So it certainly wouldn't be good for her to know about his love, in case she makes fun of it.

Why, you speak truth. I never yet saw man, / How wise, how noble, young, how rarely featur'd, / But she would spell him backward: if fair-fac'd, / She would swear the gentleman should be her sister; / If black, why, Nature, drawing of an antick, / Made a foul blot; if tall, a lance ill-headed; / If low, an agate very vilely cut; / If speaking, why, a vane blown with all winds; / If silent, why, a block moved with none. / So turns she every man the wrong side out, / And never gives to truth and virtue that / Which simpleness and merit purchaseth.

Why, you're right. I've never seen a man, however clever, noble, young or handsome, whom she wouldn't turn inside out. If he was fair-skinned, she'd swear the gentleman should be her sister. If he was dark, why, Nature was drawing a clown and made an ugly blot. If he was tall, he was a badly topped lance; if short, a tiny carved stone, very badly cut. If he talked, a weathervane blown by every wind; if he was quiet, a block of wood that nothing moves. That's how she turns every man inside out, and never gives truth and virtue the credit that honesty and merit deserve.
Sure, sure, such carping is not commendable.
Certainly, certainly, such fault-finding isn't admirable.

No; not to be so odd, and from all fashions, / As Beatrice is, cannot be commendable. / But who dare tell her so? If I should speak, / She would mock me into air: O! she would laugh me / Out of myself, press me to death with wit. / Therefore let Benedick, like cover'd fire, / Consume away in sighs, waste inwardly: / It were a better death than die with mocks, / Which is as bad as die with tickling.

No, being so odd and against all normal ways, as Beatrice is, can't be admirable. But who would dare tell her so? If I spoke up, she'd mock me into thin air. Oh, she'd laugh me out of myself and crush me to death with her wit. So let Benedick, like a smothered fire, burn away in sighs and waste away inside. That would be a better death than dying of mockery, which is as bad as being tickled to death.
Yet tell her of it: hear what she will say.
Still, tell her about it, and hear what she says.

No; rather I will go to Benedick, / And counsel him to fight against his passion. / And, truly, I'll devise some honest slanders / To stain my cousin with. One doth not know / How much an ill word may empoison liking.

No, I'd rather go to Benedick and advise him to fight his passion. And honestly, I'll invent some harmless slanders to blacken my cousin's name with. You never know how much a bad word can poison love.

O! do not do your cousin such a wrong. / She cannot be so much without true judgment,— / Having so swift and excellent a wit / As she is priz'd to have,—as to refuse / So rare a gentleman as Signior Benedick.

Oh, don't do your cousin such an injustice. She can't be so lacking in good judgment, having such a quick and excellent wit as she's famous for, as to refuse such a rare gentleman as Signior Benedick.
He is the only man of Italy, / Always excepted my dear Claudio.
He's the finest man in Italy, except of course my dear Claudio.
I pray you, be not angry with me, madam, / Speaking my fancy: Signior Benedick, / For shape, for bearing, argument and valour, / Goes foremost in report through Italy.
Please don't be angry with me, madam, for saying what I think: Signior Benedick, for his looks, his manner, his conversation and his courage, has the best reputation in all Italy.
Indeed, he hath an excellent good name.
Yes, he has an excellent reputation.
His excellence did earn it, ere he had it. / When are you married, madam?
His excellence earned it before he had it. When are you getting married, madam?
Why, every day, to-morrow. Come, go in: / I'll show thee some attires, and have thy counsel / Which is the best to furnish me to-morrow.
Why, any day now: tomorrow. Come, let's go in. I'll show you some outfits, and you can advise me which is best to wear tomorrow.
She's lim'd, I warrant you: we have caught her, madam.
She's trapped, I promise you. We've caught her, madam.
If it prove so, then loving goes by haps: / Some Cupid kills with arrows, some with traps.
If that's true, then love works by chance. Cupid kills some with arrows, some with traps.

[Advancing.] What fire is in mine ears? Can this be true? / Stand I condemn'd for pride and scorn so much? / Contempt, farewell! and maiden pride, adieu! / No glory lives behind the back of such. / And, Benedick, love on; I will requite thee, / Taming my wild heart to thy loving hand: / If thou dost love, my kindness shall incite thee / To bind our loves up in a holy band; / For others say thou dost deserve, and I / Believe it better than reportingly.

What burning is this in my ears? Can this be true? Am I so condemned for pride and scorn? Contempt, goodbye! And girlish pride, farewell! No one speaks well of such things behind your back. And, Benedick, keep loving; I'll return your love, taming my wild heart to your loving hand. If you love me, my kindness will encourage you to tie our love together with the holy bond of marriage. For other people say you deserve it, and I believe it better than just from what they say.
I do but stay till your marriage be consummate, and then go I / toward Arragon.
I'll only stay until your marriage is complete, and then I'll head for Aragon.
I'll bring you thither, my lord, if you'll vouchsafe me.
I'll go with you there, my lord, if you'll allow me.

Nay, that would be as great a soil in the new gloss of your marriage, / as to show a child his new coat and forbid him to wear it. I will only / be bold with Benedick for his company; for, from the crown of his head / to the sole of his foot, he is all mirth; he hath twice or thrice cut / Cupid's bowstring, and the little hangman dare not shoot at him. He / hath a heart as sound as a bell, and his tongue is the clapper; for / what his heart thinks his tongue speaks.

No, that would spoil the fresh shine of your marriage as much as showing a child his new coat and forbidding him to wear it. I'll only ask Benedick to come with me. From the top of his head to the soles of his feet he's all fun. He has cut Cupid's bowstring two or three times, and the little executioner doesn't dare shoot at him. He has a heart as sound as a bell, and his tongue is the clapper; whatever his heart thinks, his tongue says.
Gallants, I am not as I have been.
Gentlemen, I'm not what I used to be.
So say I: methinks you are sadder.
That's what I think: you seem more serious.
I hope he be in love.
Hang him, truant! there's no true drop of blood in him, to be truly / touched with love. If he be sad, he wants money.
Hang him, the layabout! There isn't a drop of true blood in him to be truly touched by love. If he's gloomy, he's short of money.
You must hang it first, and draw it afterwards.
You have to hang it first and then draw it, like a traitor.
Where is but a humour or a worm?
Which is only caused by a bit of fluid or a worm?
Well, every one can master a grief but he that has it.
Well, everyone can cope with a pain except the man who has it.
Yet say I, he is in love.
All the same, I say he's in love.

There is no appearance of fancy in him, unless it be a fancy that he / hath to strange disguises; as to be a Dutchman to-day, a Frenchman / to-morrow; or in the shape of two countries at once, as a German from / the waist downward, all slops, and a Spaniard from the hip upward, no / doublet. Unless he have a fancy to this foolery, as it appears he / hath, he is no fool for fancy, as you would have it appear he is.

There's no sign of fancy in him, unless it's a fancy for strange costumes: dressing as a Dutchman today, a Frenchman tomorrow, or as two countries at once, a German from the waist down, all baggy trousers, and a Spaniard from the hips up, with no jacket. Unless he has a fancy for this foolishness, as it seems he has, he's no fool for love, as you want to make out.
If he be not in love with some woman, there is no believing old signs: / a' brushes his hat a mornings; what should that bode?
If he's not in love with some woman, there's no believing the old signs. He brushes his hat every morning; what could that mean?
Hath any man seen him at the barber's?
Has anyone seen him at the barber's?
No, but the barber's man hath been seen with him; and the old / ornament of his cheek hath already stuffed tennis-balls.
No, but the barber's assistant has been seen with him, and the old decoration on his cheeks has already been used to stuff tennis balls.
Indeed he looks younger than he did, by the loss of a beard.
It's true, he looks younger without his beard.
Nay, a' rubs himself with civet: can you smell him out by that?
And he rubs himself with perfume. Can you sniff him out from that?
That's as much as to say the sweet youth's in love.
That's as good as saying the sweet youth is in love.
The greatest note of it is his melancholy.
The biggest sign of it is his gloom.
And when was he wont to wash his face?
And since when did he wash his face?
Yea, or to paint himself? for the which, I hear what they say of him.
Yes, or wear make-up? I hear what people say about that.
Nay, but his jesting spirit; which is now crept into a lute-string, / and new-governed by stops.
No, but look at his joking spirit, which has now crept into a lute-string and is controlled by its frets.
Indeed, that tells a heavy tale for him. Conclude, conclude he is / in love.
Indeed, that tells a sad story about him. Conclude, conclude: he's in love.
Nay, but I know who loves him.
No, but I know who loves him.
That would I know too: I warrant, one that knows him not.
I'd like to know that too. Someone who doesn't know him, I bet.
Yes, and his ill conditions; and in despite of all, dies for him.
Yes she does, and his bad habits too; and in spite of everything, she's dying for him.
She shall be buried with her face upwards.
Then she'll be buried face up, in her lover's arms.
Yet is this no charm for the tooth-ache. Old signior, walk aside with / me: I have studied eight or nine wise words to speak to you, which / these hobby-horses must not hear.
Still, none of this cures toothache. Old signior, walk aside with me. I've prepared eight or nine wise words to say to you, which these clowns mustn't hear.
For my life, to break with him about Beatrice.
I bet my life he's going to talk to him about Beatrice.
'Tis even so. Hero and Margaret have by this played their parts with / Beatrice, and then the two bears will not bite one another when they / meet.
That's exactly it. Hero and Margaret will have played their parts with Beatrice by now, and so the two bears won't bite each other when they meet.
My lord and brother, God save you!
My lord and brother, God save you!
If your leisure served, I would speak with you.
If you had time, I'd like to speak with you.
If it please you; yet Count Claudio may hear, for what I would / speak of concerns him.
If you like. But Count Claudio can hear, because what I want to say concerns him.
[To CLAUDIO.] Means your lordship to be married to-morrow?
Does your lordship mean to be married tomorrow?
I know not that, when he knows what I know.
I don't know that, once he knows what I know.
If there be any impediment, I pray you discover it.
If there's any obstacle, please reveal it.

You may think I love you not: let that appear hereafter, and aim / better at me by that I now will manifest. For my brother, I think / he holds you well, and in dearness of heart hath holp to effect your / ensuing marriage; surely suit ill-spent and labour ill bestowed!

You may think I don't like you. Let that be shown later, and judge me better by what I'm about to reveal. As for my brother, I think he's very fond of you, and out of affection he has helped arrange your coming marriage. Surely an effort wasted and work thrown away!
I came hither to tell you; and circumstances shortened,—for she / has been too long a talking of,—the lady is disloyal.
I came here to tell you. To cut a long story short, since she's been talked about for too long: the lady is unfaithful.
Even she: Leonato's Hero, your Hero, every man's Hero.
That's her: Leonato's Hero, your Hero, every man's Hero.

The word's too good to paint out her wickedness; I could say, she were / worse: think you of a worse title, and I will fit her to it. Wonder / not till further warrant: go but with me to-night, you shall see her / chamber-window entered, even the night before her wedding-day: if you / love her then, to-morrow wed her; but it would better fit your honour / to change your mind.

The word is too good to describe her wickedness. I could say she's worse. Think of a worse name, and I'll prove it fits her. Don't be amazed until you have more proof. Just come with me tonight, and you'll see someone climb in at her bedroom window, on the very night before her wedding. If you still love her after that, marry her tomorrow; but it would suit your honour better to change your mind.
If you dare not trust that you see, confess not that you know. If you / will follow me, I will show you enough; and when you have seen more / and heard more, proceed accordingly.
If you don't dare trust what you see, don't admit to what you know. If you follow me, I'll show you enough; and when you've seen and heard more, act on it.
If I see anything to-night why I should not marry her to-morrow, in / the congregation, where I should wed, there will I shame her.
If I see anything tonight that means I shouldn't marry her tomorrow, I'll shame her in front of the congregation where I was supposed to marry her.
And, as I wooed for thee to obtain her, I will join with thee to / disgrace her.
And since I wooed her to win her for you, I'll join you in disgracing her.
I will disparage her no farther till you are my witnesses: bear it / coldly but till midnight, and let the issue show itself.
I won't run her down any further until you are my witnesses. Stay calm until midnight, and let the outcome speak for itself.
Oh, what a day gone wrong!
O plague right well prevented! So will you say when you have seen / the sequel.
Oh, what a plague well prevented! That's what you'll say when you've seen what follows.
Are you good men and true?
Are you good men and true?
Yea, or else it were pity but they should suffer salvation, body / and soul.
Yes, or else it would be a pity if they didn't suffer salvation (he means damnation), body and soul.
Nay, that were a punishment too good for them, if they should have / any allegiance in them, being chosen for the prince's watch.
No, that would be too good a punishment for them, if they had any allegiance (he means disloyalty) in them, having been chosen for the prince's watch.
Well, give them their charge, neighbour Dogberry.
Well, give them their orders, neighbour Dogberry.
First, who think you the most desartless man to be constable?
First, who do you think is the most desertless (he means deserving) man to be constable?
Hugh Oatcake, sir, or George Seacoal; for they can write and read.
Hugh Oatcake, sir, or George Seacoal, because they can read and write.
Come hither, neighbour Seacoal. God hath blessed you with a good name: / to be a well-favoured man is the gift of fortune; but to write and / read comes by nature.
Come here, neighbour Seacoal. God has blessed you with a good name. Being good-looking is a gift of fortune, but reading and writing come by nature.

You have: I knew it would be your answer. Well, for your favour, sir, / why, give God thanks, and make no boast of it; and for your writing / and reading, let that appear when there is no need of such vanity. / You are thought here to be the most senseless and fit man for the / constable of the watch; therefore bear you the lanthorn. This is your / charge: you shall comprehend all vagrom men; you are to bid any man / stand, in the prince's name.

You have: I knew that would be your answer. Well, as for your looks, sir, thank God for them and don't boast about them; and as for your reading and writing, show them when there's no need for such vanity. You're thought to be the most senseless (he means sensible) and suitable man here to be constable of the watch, so you'll carry the lantern. These are your orders: you will comprehend (he means apprehend) all vagrant men. You're to order any man to stand still, in the prince's name.
How, if a' will not stand?
What if he won't stand still?
Why, then, take no note of him, but let him go; and presently call / the rest of the watch together, and thank God you are rid of a knave.
Why, then, take no notice of him, but let him go; and at once call the rest of the watch together and thank God you're rid of a villain.
If he will not stand when he is bidden, he is none of the prince's / subjects.
If he won't stand when he's told to, he's not one of the prince's subjects.
True, and they are to meddle with none but the prince's subjects. / You shall also make no noise in the streets: for, for the watch to / babble and to talk is most tolerable and not to be endured.

True, and they're to deal only with the prince's subjects. Also, you must make no noise in the streets; for the watch to babble and chatter is most tolerable (he means intolerable) and not to be put up with.
We will rather sleep than talk: we know what belongs to a watch.
We'll sleep rather than talk. We know what's proper for a watch.

Why, you speak like an ancient and most quiet watchman, for I / cannot see how sleeping should offend; only have a care that your / bills be not stolen. Well, you are to call at all the alehouses, / and bid those that are drunk get them to bed.

Why, you speak like an experienced and very quiet watchman, for I can't see how sleeping could do any harm. Just take care your weapons aren't stolen. Well, you're to call at all the pubs and tell those who are drunk to go to bed.
Why then, let them alone till they are sober: if they make you not / then the better answer, you may say they are not the men you took / them for.
Why then, leave them alone until they're sober. If they don't give you a better answer then, you can say they aren't the men you took them for.
If you meet a thief, you may suspect him, by virtue of your office, / to be no true man; and, for such kind of men, the less you meddle / or make with them, why, the more is for your honesty.
If you meet a thief, you may suspect him, because of your job, of being dishonest; and as for men like that, the less you have to do with them, the better for your honesty.
If we know him to be a thief, shall we not lay hands on him?
If we know he's a thief, shouldn't we arrest him?

Truly, by your office, you may; but I think they that touch pitch will / be defiled. The most peaceable way for you, if you do take a thief, is / to let him show himself what he is and steal out of your company.
Well, because of your job you may; but I think that whoever touches tar gets dirty. The most peaceful way, if you do catch a thief, is to let him show what he is and steal away from you.
You have been always called a merciful man, partner.
You've always been called a merciful man, partner.
Truly, I would not hang a dog by my will, much more a man who hath any / honesty in him.
Truly, I wouldn't willingly hang a dog, let alone a man with any honesty in him.
If you hear a child cry in the night, you must call to the nurse / and bid her still it.
If you hear a child crying in the night, you must call the nurse and tell her to quieten it.
How if the nurse be asleep and will not hear us?
What if the nurse is asleep and won't hear us?
Why then, depart in peace, and let the child wake her with crying; / for the ewe that will not hear her lamb when it baes, will never / answer a calf when he bleats.
Why then, leave in peace and let the child wake her with its crying; for the ewe that won't hear her own lamb when it baas will never answer a calf when it bleats.
This is the end of the charge. You constable, are to present the / prince's own person: if you meet the prince in the night, you may / stay him.
That's the end of your orders. You, constable, represent the prince's own person. If you meet the prince in the night, you may stop him.
Nay, by'r lady, that I think, a' cannot.
No, by Our Lady, I don't think he can.

Five shillings to one on't, with any man that knows the statutes, he / may stay him: marry, not without the prince be willing; for, indeed, / the watch ought to offend no man, and it is an offence to stay a man / against his will.

Five shillings to one on it, with any man who knows the laws: he may stop him. But not unless the prince is willing; because the watch really ought to offend nobody, and it's an offence to stop a man against his will.
By'r lady, I think it be so.
By Our Lady, I think that's right.
Ha, ah, ha! Well, masters, good night: an there be any matter of weight / chances, call up me: keep your fellows' counsels and your own, and good / night. Come, neighbour.
Ha, ha, ha! Well, men, good night. If anything important happens, wake me up. Keep your fellows' secrets and your own, and good night. Come, neighbour.
Well, masters, we hear our charge: let us go sit here upon the / church-bench till two, and then all to bed.
Well, men, we've heard our orders. Let's go and sit here on the church bench until two, and then all go to bed.
One word more, honest neighbours. I pray you, watch about Signior / Leonato's door; for the wedding being there to-morrow, there is a great / coil to-night. / Adieu; be vigitant, I beseech you.

One more word, honest neighbours. Please keep watch around Signior Leonato's door, because the wedding is there tomorrow and there's a great fuss going on tonight. Goodbye; be vigitant (he means vigilant), I beg you.
Here, man. I am at thy elbow.
Here, man. I'm right at your elbow.
Mass, and my elbow itched; I thought there would a scab follow.
By the Mass, my elbow was itching; I thought a scab would follow.
I will owe thee an answer for that; and now forward with thy tale.
I'll answer that insult later. Now get on with your story.
Stand thee close then under this penthouse, for it drizzles rain, / and I will, like a true drunkard, utter all to thee.
Stand close to me under this porch roof, then, because it's drizzling; and like a true drunkard I'll tell you everything.
[Aside.] Some treason, masters; yet stand close.
Some treason, men; but keep hidden.
Therefore know, I have earned of Don John a thousand ducats.
Well, then, I've earned a thousand ducats from Don John.
Is it possible that any villany should be so dear?
Is it possible that any villainy could be so expensive?
Thou shouldst rather ask if it were possible any villany should be / so rich; for when rich villains have need of poor ones, poor ones may / make what price they will.
You should rather ask if it's possible for any villain to be so rich; for when rich villains need poor ones, poor ones can name their price.
That shows thou art unconfirmed. Thou knowest that the fashion of / a doublet, or a hat, or a cloak, is nothing to a man.
That shows you're inexperienced. You know that the style of a jacket or a hat or a cloak means nothing about a man.
Yes, the fashion is the fashion.
Yes, the fashion is the fashion.
Tush! I may as well say the fool's the fool. But seest thou not what / a deformed thief this fashion is?
Rubbish! I might as well say a fool is a fool. But don't you see what a deformed thief this fashion is?
[Aside.] I know that Deformed; a' has been a vile thief this seven / years; a' goes up and down like a gentleman: I remember his name.
I know that Deformed. He's been a vile thief these seven years. He goes around dressed like a gentleman. I remember his name.
No: 'twas the vane on the house.
No, it was the weathervane on the house.

Seest thou not, I say, what a deformed thief this fashion is? how / giddily he turns about all the hot bloods between fourteen and / five-and-thirty? sometime fashioning them like Pharaoh's soldiers in / the reechy painting; sometime like god Bel's priests in the old / church-window; sometime like the shaven Hercules in the smirched / worm-eaten tapestry, where his codpiece seems as massy as his club?

Don't you see, I say, what a deformed thief this fashion is? How dizzily he spins round all the hot-blooded young men between fourteen and thirty-five? Sometimes dressing them like Pharaoh's soldiers in a grimy painting, sometimes like the priests of the god Bel in an old church window, sometimes like the clean-shaven Hercules in a dirty, worm-eaten tapestry, where his codpiece looks as massive as his club?

All this I see, and I see that the fashion wears out more apparel than / the man. But art not thou thyself giddy with the fashion too, that / thou hast shifted out of thy tale into telling me of the fashion?
I see all that, and I see that fashion wears out more clothes than the men do. But aren't you dizzy with fashion yourself, since you've switched from your story to telling me about fashion?

Not so neither; but know, that I have to-night wooed Margaret, the / Lady Hero's gentlewoman, by the name of Hero: she leans me out at her / mistress' chamber-window, bids me a thousand times good night,—I tell / this tale vilely:—I should first tell thee how the prince, Claudio, / and my master, planted and placed and possessed by my master Don John, / saw afar off in the orchard this amiable encounter.

Not at all. But listen: tonight I've wooed Margaret, the Lady Hero's maid, calling her Hero. She leans out of her mistress's bedroom window to me and says good night a thousand times. I'm telling this badly. I should first tell you how the prince, Claudio and my master, set up and placed and convinced by my master Don John, watched this loving meeting from a distance in the orchard.
And thought they Margaret was Hero?
And they thought Margaret was Hero?

Two of them did, the prince and Claudio; but the devil my master, knew / she was Margaret; and partly by his oaths, which first possessed them, / partly by the dark night, which did deceive them, but chiefly by my / villany, which did confirm any slander that Don John had made, away / went Claudio enraged; swore he would meet her, as he was appointed, / next morning at the temple, and there, before the whole congregation, / shame her with what he saw o'er night, and send her home again without / a husband.

Two of them did, the prince and Claudio; but the devil my master knew she was Margaret. And partly because of his oaths, which convinced them in the first place, partly because of the dark night, which fooled them, but mainly because of my villainy, which confirmed every slander Don John had told, Claudio went off furious. He swore he'd meet her next morning at the church as arranged and there, in front of the whole congregation, shame her with what he'd seen that night and send her home again without a husband.
We charge you in the prince's name, stand!
We order you in the prince's name: stand!
Call up the right Master Constable. We have here recovered the most / dangerous piece of lechery that ever was known in the commonwealth.
Call the real Master Constable. We've recovered (he means uncovered) the most dangerous piece of lechery (he means treachery) ever known in the state.
And one Deformed is one of them: I know him, a' wears a lock.
And one Deformed is one of them. I know him: he wears a lovelock.
You'll be made bring Deformed forth, I warrant you.
You'll be made to produce Deformed, I promise you.
Never speak: we charge you let us obey you to go with us.
Don't speak. We order you to let us obey you (he means you to obey us) and come with us.
We are like to prove a goodly commodity, being taken up of these / men's bills.
We're likely to be a fine bargain, bought on credit by these men's weapons.
A commodity in question, I warrant you. Come, we'll obey you.
A bargain that'll be questioned, I'm sure. Come, we'll obey you.
Good Ursula, wake my cousin Beatrice, and desire her to rise.
Good Ursula, wake my cousin Beatrice and ask her to get up.
And tell her to come here.
Troth, I think your other rabato were better.
Honestly, I think your other collar would be better.
No, pray thee, good Meg, I'll wear this.
No, please, good Meg, I'll wear this one.
By my troth's not so good; and I warrant your cousin will say so.
Honestly, it's not so good, and I bet your cousin will say so.
My cousin 's a fool, and thou art another: I'll wear none but this.
My cousin's a fool, and so are you. I'll wear only this one.
I like the new tire within excellently, if the hair were a thought / browner; and your gown 's a most rare fashion, i' faith. I saw the / Duchess of Milan's gown that they praise so.

I like the new headdress in the next room very much, if the hair were a shade browner; and your gown is a really rare fashion, honestly. I've seen the Duchess of Milan's gown that everyone praises so much.
Oh, they say that's beyond compare.

By my troth 's but a night-gown in respect of yours: cloth o' gold, / and cuts, and laced with silver, set with pearls, down sleeves, side / sleeves, and skirts round, underborne with a blush tinsel; but for a / fine, quaint, graceful, and excellent fashion, yours is worth ten on't.

Honestly, it's only a dressing gown compared with yours: cloth of gold, slashed, trimmed with silver lace, set with pearls, with long sleeves and hanging sleeves, and skirts trimmed round, lined with shimmering blue. But for a fine, elegant, graceful and excellent style, yours is worth ten of it.
God give me joy to wear it! for my heart is exceeding heavy.
God give me joy in wearing it! For my heart is very heavy.
'Twill be heavier soon by the weight of a man.
It'll soon be heavier with the weight of a man.
Fie upon thee! art not ashamed?
Shame on you! Aren't you ashamed?

Of what, lady? of speaking honourably? is not marriage honourable in a / beggar? Is not your lord honourable without marriage? I think you / would have me say, 'saving your reverence, a husband:' an bad thinking / do not wrest true speaking, I'll offend nobody. / Is there any harm in 'the heavier for a husband'? None, I think, an it / be the right husband and the right wife; otherwise 'tis light, and not / heavy: ask my Lady Beatrice else; here she comes.

Of what, lady? Of speaking honourably? Isn't marriage honourable, even for a beggar? Isn't your lord honourable, marriage or not? I think you'd want me to say, 'begging your pardon, a husband'. If dirty minds don't twist honest words, I'll offend nobody. Is there any harm in 'the heavier for a husband'? None, I think, if it's the right husband and the right wife; otherwise it's light, not heavy. Ask my Lady Beatrice if you don't believe me; here she comes.
Why, how now? do you speak in the sick tune?
Why, what's this? Are you speaking in a sickly tone?
I am out of all other tune, methinks.
I seem to be out of tune for anything else.
Clap's into 'Light o' love'; that goes without a burden: do you sing / it, and I'll dance it.
Let's strike up 'Light o' Love'; it has no bass part. You sing it and I'll dance it.
Ye, light o' love with your heels! then, if your husband have stables / enough, you'll see he shall lack no barnes.
Yes, 'Light o' Love' with your heels! Then if your husband has stables enough, you'll see he won't be short of babies.
O illegitimate construction! I scorn that with my heels.
Oh, what a disgraceful interpretation! I kick that away with my heels.
'Tis almost five o'clock, cousin; 'tis time you were ready. By my / troth, I am exceeding ill. Heigh-ho!
It's almost five o'clock, cousin; it's time you were ready. Honestly, I feel really ill. Oh dear!
For a hawk, a horse, or a husband?
Are you sighing for a hawk, a horse or a husband?
For the letter that begins them all, H.
For the letter they all begin with: H (an 'ache').
Well, an you be not turned Turk, there's no more sailing by the star.
Well, if you haven't converted to a new faith, there's no steering by the stars any more.
What does the fool mean, I wonder?
Nothing I; but God send every one their heart's desire!
Nothing, me; but God give everyone their heart's desire!
These gloves the Count sent me; they are an excellent perfume.
The count sent me these gloves. They have an excellent perfume.
I am stuffed, cousin, I cannot smell.
I'm all stuffed up, cousin. I can't smell.
A maid, and stuffed! there's goodly catching of cold.
A virgin, and stuffed! That's a fine way to catch a cold.
O, God help me! God help me! how long have you professed / apprehension?
Oh, God help me, God help me! How long have you been claiming to be witty?
Ever since you left it. Doth not my wit become me rarely!
Ever since you gave it up. Doesn't my wit suit me beautifully?
It is not seen enough, you should wear it in your cap. By my troth, / I am sick.
It isn't seen enough; you should wear it in your cap, like a fool. Honestly, I'm ill.
Get you some of this distilled Carduus Benedictus, and lay it to / your heart: it is the only thing for a qualm.
Get some of this distilled holy thistle, Carduus Benedictus, and put it on your heart. It's the only cure for queasiness.
There thou prick'st her with a thistle.
There, you've pricked her with a thistle.
Benedictus! why benedictus? you have some moral in this Benedictus.
Benedictus! Why Benedictus? You have some hidden meaning in this Benedictus.

Moral! no, by my troth, I have no moral meaning; I meant, plain / holy-thistle. You may think, perchance, that I think you are in love: / nay, by'r lady, I am not such a fool to think what I list; nor I list / not to think what I can; nor, indeed, I cannot think, if I would think / my heart out of thinking, that you are in love, or that you will be in / love, or that you can be in love. / Yet Benedick was such another, and now is he become a man: he swore he / would never marry; and yet now, in despite of his heart, he eats his / meat without grudging: and how you may be converted, I know not; but / methinks you look with your eyes as other women do.

Hidden meaning! No, honestly, I have no hidden meaning. I meant plain holy thistle. You may perhaps think that I think you're in love. No, by Our Lady, I'm not such a fool as to think whatever I like; and I don't like to think whatever I can; and in fact I couldn't think, even if I thought my heart out, that you're in love, or that you will be in love, or that you can be in love. Still, Benedick was the same, and now he has become a man like any other. He swore he'd never marry, and yet now, in spite of himself, he eats his food without complaining. How you might be converted, I don't know; but it seems to me you look with your eyes the way other women do.
What pace is this that thy tongue keeps?
What pace is this your tongue is running at?
Not a false gallop: it's a true one.
Madam, withdraw: the prince, the count, Signior Benedick, Don John, / and all the gallants of the town, are come to fetch you to church.
Madam, come away. The prince, the count, Signior Benedick, Don John and all the young gentlemen of the town have come to take you to church.
Help to dress me, good coz, good Meg, good Ursula.
Help me get dressed, good cousin, good Meg, good Ursula.
What would you with me, honest neighbour?
What do you want with me, honest neighbour?
Marry, sir, I would have some confidence with you, that decerns / you nearly.
Well, sir, I'd like to have a confidence (he means conference) with you that decerns (concerns) you closely.
Brief, I pray you; for you see it is a busy time with me.
Be brief, please, because as you see, I'm very busy.
Yes, in truth it is, sir.
What is it, my good friends?
What is it, my good friends?
Goodman Verges, sir, speaks a little off the matter: an old man, / sir, and his wits are not so blunt as, God help, I would desire / they were; but, in faith, honest as the skin between his brows.

Goodman Verges, sir, wanders off the point a bit. He's an old man, sir, and his wits are not as blunt (he means sharp) as I'd like them to be, God help him; but honestly, he's as honest as the skin between his eyebrows.
Yes, I thank God, I am as honest as any man living, that is an / old man and no honester than I.
Yes, thank God, I'm as honest as any man alive who is an old man and no more honest than me.
Comparisons are odorous: palabras, neighbour Verges.
Comparisons are odorous (he means odious). Palabras: few words, neighbour Verges.
It pleases your worship to say so, but we are the poor duke's / officers; but truly, for mine own part, if I were as tedious as / a king, I could find in my heart to bestow it all of your worship.
Your worship is kind to say so, but we are only the poor duke's officers. But honestly, for my part, if I were as tedious as a king, I'd gladly give it all to your worship.
All thy tediousness on me! ha?
All your tediousness to me, eh?
Yea, an 't were a thousand pound more than 'tis; for I hear as good / exclamation on your worship, as of any man in the city, and though / I be but a poor man, I am glad to hear it.

Yes, even if it were a thousand pounds more than it is; for I hear as good exclamation (he means acclamation) about your worship as about any man in the city, and though I'm only a poor man, I'm glad to hear it.
I would fain know what you have to say.
I'd really like to know what you have to say.
Marry, sir, our watch to-night, excepting your worship's presence, / ha' ta'en a couple of as arrant knaves as any in Messina.
Well, sir, our watch tonight, excepting (he means respecting) your worship's presence, has caught a pair of the biggest villains in Messina.

A good old man, sir; he will be talking; as they say, 'when the age is / in, the wit is out.' God help us! it is a world to see! Well said, i' / faith, neighbour Verges: well, God's a good man; an two men ride of a / horse, one must ride behind. An honest soul, i' faith, sir; by my / troth he is, as ever broke bread; but God is to be worshipped: all men / are not alike; alas! good neighbour.

A good old man, sir; he will keep talking. As they say, 'When age comes in, wit goes out.' God help us! What a world it is! Well said, really, neighbour Verges. Well, God's a good man. If two men ride one horse, one must ride behind. An honest soul, really, sir; upon my word he is, as honest as anyone who ever broke bread. But God be praised, all men aren't alike. Ah well, good neighbour!
Indeed, neighbour, he comes too short of you.
Indeed, neighbour, he falls a long way short of you.
One word, sir: our watch, sir, hath indeed comprehended two / aspicious persons, and we would have them this morning examined / before your worship.
One word, sir. Our watch, sir, has indeed comprehended (apprehended) two aspicious (suspicious) persons, and we'd like them examined in front of your worship this morning.
Take their examination yourself, and bring it me: I am now in great / haste, as may appear unto you.
Question them yourself and bring me the report. I'm in a great hurry now, as you can see.
It will be suffigance (he means sufficient).
Drink some wine ere you go: fare you well.
Have some wine before you go. Goodbye.
My lord, they stay for you to give your daughter to her husband.
My lord, they're waiting for you to give your daughter to her husband.
I'll wait upon them: I am ready.
I'll come to them. I'm ready.
Go, good partner, go, get you to Francis Seacoal; bid him bring his / pen and inkhorn to the gaol: we are now to examination these men.
Go, good partner, go to Francis Seacoal. Tell him to bring his pen and ink to the jail. We're going to examination these men now.
And we must do it wisely.
And we must do it wisely.
We will spare for no wit, I warrant you; here's that shall drive some / of them to a non-come: only get the learned writer to set down our / excommunication, and meet me at the gaol.

We won't spare any wit, I promise you. Here's something that will drive some of them to a non-come (he means non plus, a loss for words). Just get the learned clerk to write down our excommunication (he means communication), and meet me at the jail.
Come, Friar Francis, be brief: only to the plain form of marriage, / and you shall recount their particular duties afterwards.
Come, Friar Francis, be brief. Just the basic marriage service; you can explain their particular duties to them afterwards.
You come hither, my lord, to marry this lady?
You come here, my lord, to marry this lady?
To be married to her, friar; you come to marry her.
To be married to her, friar; you are the one who marries her.
Lady, you come hither to be married to this count?
Lady, you come here to be married to this count?
If either of you know any inward impediment, why you should not be / conjoined, I charge you, on your souls, to utter it.
If either of you knows any secret obstacle why you should not be joined, I order you, on your souls, to say it.
Do you know of any, Hero?
Do you know of any, count?
I dare make his answer; none.
I'll dare to answer for him: none.
O! what men dare do! what men may do! what men daily do, not / knowing what they do!
Oh, what men dare to do! What men may do! What men do every day, not knowing what they're doing!
How now! Interjections? Why then, some be of laughing, as ah! ha! / he!
Well! Exclamations? Then let's have some laughing ones, like 'ah! ha! he!'
Stand thee by, friar. Father, by your leave: Will you with free and / unconstrained soul Give me this maid, your daughter?
Stand aside, friar. Father, excuse me: will you, freely and without any pressure, give me this girl, your daughter?
As freely, son, as God did give her me.
As freely, son, as God gave her to me.
And what have I to give you back whose worth / May counterpoise this rich and precious gift?
And what can I give you back that is worth as much as this rich and precious gift?
Nothing, unless you render her again.
Nothing, unless you give her back again.

Sweet prince, you learn me noble thankfulness. / There, Leonato, take her back again: / Give not this rotten orange to your friend; / She's but the sign and semblance of her honour. / Behold! how like a maid she blushes here. / O! what authority and show of truth / Can cunning sin cover itself withal. / Comes not that blood as modest evidence / To witness simple virtue? Would you not swear, / All you that see her, that she were a maid, / By these exterior shows? But she is none: / She knows the heat of a luxurious bed; / Her blush is guiltiness, not modesty.

Sweet prince, you teach me noble gratitude. There, Leonato, take her back again. Don't give this rotten orange to your friend; she only looks honourable on the outside. Look how she blushes here like a virgin! Oh, how clever sin can disguise itself with such an air of authority and truth! Doesn't that blush come as modest evidence of simple innocence? Wouldn't all of you who see her swear she was a virgin, judging by these outward signs? But she is not. She knows the heat of a lustful bed. Her blush is guilt, not modesty.
What do you mean, my lord?
What do you mean, my lord?
Not to be married, / Not to knit my soul to an approved wanton.
I mean not to be married, not to bind my soul to a proven slut.
Dear my lord, if you, in your own proof, / Have vanquish'd the resistance of her youth, / And made defeat of her virginity,—
My dear lord, if you yourself have overcome her young resistance and taken her virginity,—

I know what you would say: if I have known her, / You'll say she did embrace me as a husband, / And so extenuate the forehand sin: No, Leonato, / I never tempted her with word too large; / But, as a brother to his sister, show'd / Bashful sincerity and comely love.

I know what you're going to say. If I've slept with her, you'll say she accepted me as her husband, and so excuse the sin of doing it early. No, Leonato. I never tempted her with any improper word; but like a brother to his sister, I showed shy sincerity and decent love.
And seem'd I ever otherwise to you?
And did I ever seem any different to you?

Out on thee! Seeming! I will write against it: / You seem to me as Dian in her orb, / As chaste as is the bud ere it be blown; / But you are more intemperate in your blood / Than Venus, or those pamper'd animals / That rage in savage sensuality.

Curse you! 'Seem'! I'll write against it. You seem to me like Diana, goddess of chastity, in her sphere, as chaste as a bud before it opens. But you are more uncontrolled in your lust than Venus, or those overfed animals that rage in wild sensuality.
Is my lord well, that he doth speak so wide?
Is my lord ill, that he talks so wildly?
Sweet prince, why speak not you?
Sweet prince, why don't you speak?
What should I speak? / I stand dishonour'd, that have gone about / To link my dear friend to a common stale.
What could I say? I'm dishonoured, having tried to join my dear friend to a common prostitute.
Are these things spoken, or do I but dream?
Are these things really being said, or am I dreaming?
Sir, they are spoken, and these things are true.
Sir, they are being said, and these things are true.
This looks not like a nuptial.
This doesn't look like a wedding.
Leonato, stand I here? Is this the prince? / Is this the prince's brother? / Is this face Hero's? Are our eyes our own?
Leonato, am I standing here? Is this the prince? Is this the prince's brother? Is this Hero's face? Are our eyes our own?
All this is so; but what of this, my lord?
All this is so; but what about it, my lord?
Let me but move one question to your daughter, / And by that fatherly and kindly power / That you have in her, bid her answer truly.
Let me ask your daughter just one question, and by the natural power you have over her as her father, order her to answer truthfully.
I charge thee do so, as thou art my child.
I order you to do so, as you are my child.
O, God defend me! how am I beset! / What kind of catechizing call you this?
Oh, God protect me! How I'm surrounded! What kind of interrogation do you call this?
To make you answer truly to your name.
To make you answer truthfully to your name.
Is it not Hero? Who can blot that name / With any just reproach?
Isn't it Hero? Who can stain that name with any fair accusation?
Marry, that can Hero: / Hero itself can blot out Hero's virtue. / What man was he talk'd with you yesternight / Out at your window, betwixt twelve and one? / Now, if you are a maid, answer to this.
Why, Hero can. Hero herself can stain Hero's virtue. Who was the man who talked with you last night at your window, between twelve and one? Now, if you are a virgin, answer this.
I talk'd with no man at that hour, my lord.
I talked with no man at that hour, my lord.

Why, then are you no maiden. / Leonato, I am sorry you must hear: upon my honour, / Myself, my brother, and this grieved count, / Did see her, hear her, at that hour last night, / Talk with a ruffian at her chamber-window; / Who hath indeed, most like a liberal villain, / Confess'd the vile encounters they have had / A thousand times in secret.

Why, then, you are no virgin. Leonato, I'm sorry you have to hear this. Upon my honour, I, my brother and this grieving count saw her, and heard her, at that hour last night, talking with a ruffian at her bedroom window; and he has, like a foul-mouthed villain, confessed the vile meetings they've had a thousand times in secret.

Fie, fie! they are not to be nam'd, my lord, / Not to be spoke of; / There is not chastity enough in language / Without offence to utter them. Thus, pretty lady, / I am sorry for thy much misgovernment.

Shame, shame! They're not to be named, my lord, not to be spoken of. There aren't enough clean words in the language to describe them without offence. So, pretty lady, I'm sorry for your wicked behaviour.

O Hero! what a Hero hadst thou been, / If half thy outward graces had been plac'd / About thy thoughts and counsels of thy heart! / But fare thee well, most foul, most fair! farewell, / Thou pure impiety, and impious purity! / For thee I'll lock up all the gates of love, / And on my eyelids shall conjecture hang, / To turn all beauty into thoughts of harm, / And never shall it more be gracious.

Oh Hero! What a Hero you would have been, if half your outward beauty had been given to your thoughts and the plans of your heart! But goodbye, most foul and most beautiful! Goodbye, you pure wickedness and wicked purity! Because of you I'll lock up all the gates of love, and suspicion will hang on my eyelids, turning all beauty into thoughts of evil, and it will never seem lovely again.
Hath no man's dagger here a point for me?
Hasn't any man here got a dagger point for me?
Why, how now, cousin! wherefore sink you down?
Why, what's wrong, cousin? Why are you falling down?
Come, let us go. These things, come thus to light, / Smother her spirits up.
Come, let's go. These things, coming to light like this, have overwhelmed her.
Dead, I think! help, uncle! Hero! why, Hero! Uncle! Signior / Benedick! Friar!
Dead, I think! Help, uncle! Hero! Hero! Uncle! Signior Benedick! Friar!
O Fate! take not away thy heavy hand: / Death is the fairest cover for her shame / That may be wish'd for.
Oh Fate, don't lift your heavy hand! Death is the best covering for her shame that anyone could wish for.

Wherefore! Why, doth not every earthly thing / Cry shame upon her? Could she here deny / The story that is printed in her blood? / Do not live, Hero; do not ope thine eyes; / For, did I think thou wouldst not quickly die, / Thought I thy spirits were stronger than thy shames, / Myself would, on the rearward of reproaches, / Strike at thy life. Griev'd I, I had but one? / Chid I for that at frugal nature's frame? / O! one too much by thee. Why had I one? / Why ever wast thou lovely in mine eyes? / Why had I not with charitable hand / Took up a beggar's issue at my gates, / Who smirched thus, and mir'd with infamy, / I might have said, 'No part of it is mine; / This shame derives itself from unknown loins?' / But mine, and mine I lov'd, and mine I prais'd, / And mine that I was proud on, mine so much / That I myself was to myself not mine, / Valuing of her; why, she—O! she is fallen / Into a pit of ink, that the wide sea / Hath drops too few to wash her clean again, / And salt too little which may season give / To her foul-tainted flesh.

Why! Doesn't everything on earth cry shame on her? Could she deny the story that's written in her blushes? Don't live, Hero; don't open your eyes. For if I thought you wouldn't die quickly, if I thought your spirit was stronger than your shame, I'd strike at your life myself, after all these reproaches. Did I grieve that I had only one child? Did I blame nature for being so mean? Oh, you were one too many! Why did I have even one? Why were you ever lovely in my eyes? Why didn't I take in some beggar's child at my gates out of charity? Then, if she were stained like this and smeared with disgrace, I could have said, 'None of it is mine; this shame comes from unknown parents.' But mine, and mine I loved, and mine I praised, and mine I was proud of, mine so much that I valued her more than myself: why, she, oh, she has fallen into a pit of ink, so deep that the wide sea hasn't enough drops to wash her clean again, nor enough salt to preserve her rotten flesh.
Sir, sir, be patient. / For my part, I am so attir'd in wonder, / I know not what to say.
Sir, sir, be patient. For my part, I'm so wrapped in amazement I don't know what to say.
O! on my soul, my cousin is belied!
Oh, on my soul, my cousin has been lied about!
Lady, were you her bedfellow last night?
Lady, did you share her bed last night?
No, truly, not; although, until last night I have this / twelvemonth been her bedfellow.
No, actually, I didn't; although until last night I've shared her bed for the past year.

Confirm'd, confirm'd! O! that is stronger made, / Which was before barr'd up with ribs of iron. / Would the two princes lie? and Claudio lie, / Who lov'd her so, that, speaking of her foulness, / Wash'd it with tears? Hence from her! let her die.

Confirmed, confirmed! Oh, that makes the case even stronger, when it was already locked up with iron bars. Would the two princes lie? And would Claudio lie, who loved her so much that he wept as he spoke of her filth? Get away from her! Let her die.

Hear me a little; / For I have only been silent so long, / And given way unto this course of fortune, / By noting of the lady: I have mark'd / A thousand blushing apparitions / To start into her face; a thousand innocent shames / In angel whiteness bear away those blushes; / And in her eye there hath appear'd a fire, / To burn the errors that these princes hold / Against her maiden truth. Call me a fool; / Trust not my reading nor my observations, / Which with experimental seal doth warrant / The tenure of my book; trust not my age, / My reverence, calling, nor divinity, / If this sweet lady lie not guiltless here / Under some biting error.

Listen to me for a moment. I've only kept quiet so long and let things take their course because I've been watching the lady. I've seen a thousand blushes leap into her face, and a thousand innocent signs of shame drive those blushes away in angelic whiteness. And a fire has appeared in her eye to burn up the mistakes these princes hold against her innocence. Call me a fool. Don't trust my learning or my observations, which experience has confirmed as true. Don't trust my age, my respect, my calling or my holy office, if this sweet lady isn't lying here innocent of some cruel error.

Friar, it cannot be. / Thou seest that all the grace that she hath left / Is that she will not add to her damnation / A sin of perjury: she not denies it. / Why seek'st thou then to cover with excuse / That which appears in proper nakedness?

Friar, it can't be. You see that the only virtue she has left is that she won't add the sin of lying under oath to her damnation. She doesn't deny it. So why are you trying to cover up with excuses what is plain to see?
Lady, what man is he you are accus'd of?
Lady, who is the man you are accused of being with?

They know that do accuse me, I know none; / If I know more of any man alive / Than that which maiden modesty doth warrant, / Let all my sins lack mercy! O, my father! / Prove you that any man with me convers'd / At hours unmeet, or that I yesternight / Maintain'd the change of words with any creature, / Refuse me, hate me, torture me to death.

Those who accuse me know. I know of none. If I know more of any living man than a virgin's modesty allows, let all my sins go without mercy! Oh, my father, if you can prove that any man talked with me at improper hours, or that I exchanged words with anyone last night, disown me, hate me, torture me to death.
There is some strange misprision in the princes.
The princes have made some strange mistake.
Two of them have the very bent of honour; / And if their wisdoms be misled in this, / The practice of it lives in John the bastard, / Whose spirits toil in frame of villanies.
Two of them are completely honourable. If their judgment has been misled in this, the plot must come from John the bastard, whose mind is always busy inventing villainy.

I know not. If they speak but truth of her, / These hands shall tear her; if they wrong her honour, / The proudest of them shall well hear of it. / Time hath not yet so dried this blood of mine, / Nor age so eat up my invention, / Nor fortune made such havoc of my means, / Nor my bad life reft me so much of friends, / But they shall find, awak'd in such a kind, / Both strength of limb and policy of mind, / Ability in means and choice of friends, / To quit me of them throughly.

I don't know. If they're telling the truth about her, these hands will tear her apart. If they're wronging her honour, the proudest of them will hear from me. Time hasn't yet dried my blood so much, nor age eaten up my wits, nor bad luck so ruined my wealth, nor a bad life robbed me of so many friends, that they won't find, when I'm roused in this way, strength in my arms and cunning in my mind, enough wealth and well-chosen friends to pay them back in full.

Pause awhile, And let my counsel sway you in this case. / Your daughter here the princes left for dead; / Let her awhile be secretly kept in, / And publish it that she is dead indeed: / Maintain a mourning ostentation; / And on your family's old monument / Hang mournful epitaphs and do all rites / That appertain unto a burial.

Wait a moment, and let my advice guide you in this. The princes left your daughter here for dead. Let her be kept secretly at home for a while, and announce that she really is dead. Put on a show of mourning, hang sad epitaphs on your family's old tomb, and carry out all the rites that belong to a burial.
What shall become of this? What will this do?
What will come of this? What will this achieve?

Marry, this well carried shall on her behalf / Change slander to remorse; that is some good. / But not for that dream I on this strange course, / But on this travail look for greater birth. / She dying, as it must be so maintain'd, / Upon the instant that she was accus'd, / Shall be lamented, pitied and excus'd / Of every hearer; for it so falls out / That what we have we prize not to the worth / Whiles we enjoy it, but being lack'd and lost, / Why, then we rack the value, then we find / The virtue that possession would not show us / Whiles it was ours. So will it fare with Claudio: / When he shall hear she died upon his words, / The idea of her life shall sweetly creep / Into his study of imagination, / And every lovely organ of her life / Shall come apparell'd in more precious habit, / More moving-delicate, and full of life / Into the eye and prospect of his soul, / Than when she liv'd indeed: then shall he mourn,— / If ever love had interest in his liver,— / And wish he had not so accused her, / No, though be thought his accusation true. / Let this be so, and doubt not but success / Will fashion the event in better shape / Than I can lay it down in likelihood. / But if all aim but this be levell'd false, / The supposition of the lady's death / Will quench the wonder of her infamy: / And if it sort not well, you may conceal her,— / As best befits her wounded reputation,— / In some reclusive and religious life, / Out of all eyes, tongues, minds, and injuries.

Well, if this is handled well, it will turn slander into regret on her behalf; that's something good. But that isn't why I dream up this strange plan; I hope this labour will give birth to something greater. If it is announced that she died the moment she was accused, every listener will mourn, pity and excuse her. For it happens that we don't value what we have properly while we enjoy it, but once it's missing and lost, why, then we stretch its value to the limit; then we find the virtue that owning it wouldn't show us while it was ours. That's how it will be with Claudio. When he hears she died because of his words, the memory of her life will creep sweetly into his imagination, and every lovely part of her will come back dressed in finer clothes, more moving, more delicate and more full of life in his mind's eye than when she was really alive. Then he'll mourn, if love ever touched his heart, and wish he hadn't accused her, even if he still thought his accusation was true. Let this be done, and have no doubt that the outcome will shape things better than I can predict. And even if everything else misses its aim, the belief that the lady is dead will put an end to talk of her disgrace. And if things don't turn out well, you can hide her away, as best suits her damaged reputation, in some secluded religious life as a nun, far from all eyes, tongues, minds and harm.

Signior Leonato, let the friar advise you: / And though you know my inwardness and love / Is very much unto the prince and Claudio, / Yet, by mine honour, I will deal in this / As secretly and justly as your soul / Should with your body.

Signior Leonato, let the friar advise you. And though you know my close friendship and love belong to the prince and Claudio, still, on my honour, I'll act in this as secretly and fairly as your soul would with your own body.
Being that I flow in grief, The smallest twine may lead me.
Since I'm drowning in grief, the thinnest thread can lead me.
'Tis well consented: presently away; / For to strange sores strangely they strain the cure. / Come, lady, die to live: this wedding day / Perhaps is but prolong'd: have patience and endure.
That's well agreed. Let's go at once, for strange wounds need strange cures. Come, lady, die so that you may live. This wedding day is perhaps only postponed. Be patient and endure.
Lady Beatrice, have you wept all this while?
Lady Beatrice, have you been crying all this time?
Yea, and I will weep a while longer.
Yes, and I'll cry a while longer.
You have no reason; I do it freely.
You've no reason to; I'm doing it of my own accord.
Surely I do believe your fair cousin is wronged.
I truly believe your lovely cousin has been wronged.
Ah! how much might the man deserve of me that would right her.
Ah! How much the man who put her right would deserve from me!
Is there any way to show such friendship?
Is there any way to show such friendship?
A very even way, but no such friend.
A very simple way, but no such friend.
It is a man's office, but not yours.
It's a man's job, but not yours.
I do love nothing in the world so well as you: is not that / strange?
I love nothing in the world as much as you. Isn't that strange?

As strange as the thing I know not. It were as possible for me to say / I loved nothing so well as you; but believe me not, and yet I lie not; / I confess nothing, nor I deny nothing. I am sorry for my cousin.

As strange as something I don't know about. It would be just as possible for me to say I loved nothing as much as you. But don't believe me; and yet I'm not lying. I confess nothing, and I deny nothing. I'm sorry for my cousin.
By my sword, Beatrice, thou lovest me.
By my sword, Beatrice, you love me.
Do not swear by it, and eat it.
Don't swear by it and then eat your words.
I will swear by it that you love me; and I will make him eat it that / says I love not you.
I'll swear by it that you love me, and I'll make anyone who says I don't love you eat it.
Will you not eat your word?
With no sauce that can be devised to it. I protest I love thee.
Not with any sauce that could be invented for them. I declare I love you.
You have stayed me in a happy hour: I was about to protest I loved / you.
You interrupted me at a lucky moment. I was about to declare that I loved you.
And do it with all thy heart.
Then do it with all your heart.
I love you with so much of my heart that none is left to protest.
I love you with so much of my heart that there's none left to declare it with.
Come, bid me do anything for thee.
Come, tell me to do anything for you.
Ha! not for the wide world.
Ha! Not for the whole world.
You kill me to deny it. Farewell.
You kill me by refusing. Goodbye.
I am gone, though I am here: there is no love in you: nay, I pray / you, let me go.
I'm gone, even though I'm still here. There's no love in you. No, please, let me go.
You dare easier be friends with me than fight with mine enemy.
You find it easier to be friends with me than to fight my enemy.

Is he not approved in the height a villain, that hath slandered, / scorned, dishonoured my kinswoman? O! that I were a man. What! bear / her in hand until they come to take hands, and then, with public / accusation, uncovered slander, unmitigated rancour,—O God, that I / were a man! I would eat his heart in the market-place.

Hasn't he proved himself the worst kind of villain, who has slandered, scorned and dishonoured my cousin? Oh, if only I were a man! What! Lead her on until the moment they join hands, and then, with a public accusation, open slander, unrelenting hatred... Oh God, if only I were a man! I'd eat his heart in the market place.
Talk with a man out at a window! a proper saying!
Talking with a man at a window! A likely story!
Sweet Hero! she is wronged, she is slandered, she is undone.
Sweet Hero! She's wronged, she's slandered, she's ruined.

Princes and counties! Surely, a princely testimony, a goodly Count / Comfect; a sweet gallant, surely! O! that I were a man for his sake, / or that I had any friend would be a man for my sake! / But manhood is melted into cursies, valour into compliment, and men / are only turned into tongue, and trim ones too: he is now as valiant / as Hercules, that only tells a lie and swears it. I cannot be a man / with wishing, therefore I will die a woman with grieving.

Princes and counts! What princely evidence! What a fine Count Sugar-Sweet, a sweet gentleman, surely! Oh, if only I were a man for his sake, or had a friend who'd be a man for my sake! But manhood has melted into bowing and curtsying, courage into compliments, and men have turned into nothing but tongues, and fancy ones too. A man is now as brave as Hercules if he only tells a lie and swears it's true. I can't become a man by wishing, so I'll die a woman, grieving.
Tarry, good Beatrice. By this hand, I love thee.
Wait, good Beatrice. By this hand, I love you.
Use it for my love some other way than swearing by it.
Use it for my love in some other way than swearing by it.
Think you in your soul the Count Claudio hath wronged Hero?
Do you believe in your soul that Count Claudio has wronged Hero?
Yea, as sure is I have a thought or a soul.
Yes, as surely as I have a thought or a soul.

Enough! I am engaged, I will challenge him. I will kiss your hand, / and so leave you. By this hand, Claudio shall render me a dear account. / As you hear of me, so think of me. Go, comfort your cousin: I must / say she is dead; and so, farewell.

Enough! I'm committed. I'll challenge him. I'll kiss your hand and leave you. By this hand, Claudio will pay me dearly. Judge me by what you hear of me. Go and comfort your cousin. I must say she is dead. And so, goodbye.
Has our whole dissembly (he means assembly) appeared?
O! a stool and a cushion for the sexton.
Oh, a stool and a cushion for the clerk.
Marry, that am I and my partner.
Why, that's me and my partner.
Nay, that's certain: we have the exhibition to examine.
Yes, that's certain: we have the exhibition (he means commission) to examine them.
But which are the offenders that are to be examined? let them / come before Master constable.
But which are the offenders who are to be examined? Bring them before the Master Constable.
Yea, marry, let them come before me. What is your name, friend?
Yes, indeed, bring them before me. What's your name, friend?
Pray write down Borachio. Yours, sirrah?
I am a gentleman, sir, and my name is Conrade.
I'm a gentleman, sir, and my name is Conrade.
Write down Master gentleman Conrade. Masters, do you serve God?
Write down 'Master gentleman Conrade'. Gentlemen, do you serve God?
