Write down that they hope they serve God: and write God first; for / God defend but God should go before such villains! Masters, it is / proved already that you are little better than false knaves, and it / will go near to be thought so shortly. How answer you for yourselves?

Write down that they hope they serve God; and write God first, for God forbid that God shouldn't come before such villains! Gentlemen, it's already proved that you're little better than lying villains, and it will soon be close to being thought so. How do you answer for yourselves?
Marry, sir, we say we are none.
Well, sir, we say we're not.
A marvellous witty fellow, I assure you; but I will go about with him. / Come you hither, sirrah; a word in your ear: sir, I say to you, it is / thought you are false knaves.
A wonderfully clever fellow, I assure you; but I'll get round him. Come here, fellow, a word in your ear. Sir, I tell you, it's thought you are lying villains.
Sir, I say to you we are none.
Sir, I tell you we're not.
Well, stand aside. Fore God, they are both in a tale. Have you writ / down, that they are none?
Well, stand aside. By God, they've both got the same story. Have you written down that they're not?
Master constable, you go not the way to examine: you must call forth / the watch that are their accusers.
Master Constable, this isn't the way to question them. You must call the watchmen who are their accusers.
Yea, marry, that's the eftest way. Let the watch come forth. / Masters, I charge you, in the prince's name, accuse these men.
Yes, indeed, that's the eftest (he means deftest, quickest) way. Let the watch come forward. Men, I order you in the prince's name, accuse these men.
This man said, sir, that Don John, the prince's brother, was a / villain.
This man said, sir, that Don John, the prince's brother, was a villain.
Write down Prince John a villain. Why, this is flat perjury, to / call a prince's brother villain.
Write down 'Prince John a villain'. Why, this is plain perjury, calling a prince's brother a villain.
Pray thee, fellow, peace: I do not like thy look, I promise thee.
Please be quiet, fellow. I don't like your looks, I can tell you.
What heard you him say else?
What else did you hear him say?
Marry, that he had received a thousand ducats of Don John for / accusing the Lady Hero wrongfully.
Why, that he'd received a thousand ducats from Don John for falsely accusing the Lady Hero.
Flat burglary as ever was committed.
As plain a burglary as was ever committed.
Yea, by the mass, that it is.
Yes, by the Mass, that's right.
And that Count Claudio did mean, upon his words, to disgrace Hero / before the whole assembly, and not marry her.
And that Count Claudio intended, on his word, to disgrace Hero in front of the whole congregation and not marry her.
O villain! thou wilt be condemned into everlasting redemption for / this.
Oh, villain! You'll be condemned to everlasting redemption (he means damnation) for this.

And this is more, masters, than you can deny. Prince John is this / morning secretly stolen away: Hero was in this manner accused, in this / manner refused, and, upon the grief of this, suddenly died. Master / Constable, let these men be bound, and brought to Leonato's: I will go / before and show him their examination.

And this is more, gentlemen, than you can deny. Prince John secretly ran away this morning. Hero was accused in this way, rejected in this way, and died suddenly of grief. Master Constable, have these men tied up and brought to Leonato's. I'll go ahead and show him their statements.
Come on, have them opinioned (he means pinioned, tied up).
Let them be in the hands—
Let them be in the hands—
God's my life! where's the sexton? let him write down the prince's / officer coxcomb. Come, bind them. Thou naughty varlet!
God save my life! Where's the clerk? Let him write down that the prince's officer is a fool. Come, tie them up. You wicked rascal!
Away! you are an ass; you are an ass.
Get away! You're an ass, you're an ass.

Dost thou not suspect my place? Dost thou not suspect my years? O that / he were here to write me down an ass! but, masters, remember that I am / an ass; though it be not written down, yet forget not that I am an / ass. No, thou villain, thou art full of piety, as shall be proved upon / thee by good witness. / I am a wise fellow; and, which is more, an officer; and, which is / more, a householder; and, which is more, as pretty a piece of flesh as / any in Messina; and one that knows the law, go to; and a rich fellow / enough, go to; and a fellow that hath had losses; and one that hath / two gowns, and everything handsome about him. Bring him away. O that I / had been writ down an ass!

Don't you suspect (he means respect) my position? Don't you suspect my age? Oh, if only he were here to write me down as an ass! But, gentlemen, remember that I am an ass. Though it isn't written down, don't forget that I am an ass. No, you villain, you're full of piety (he means impiety), as good witnesses will prove against you. I'm a wise fellow; and what's more, an officer; and what's more, a householder; and what's more, as fine a piece of flesh as any in Messina; and one who knows the law, so there; and quite a rich fellow, so there; and a fellow who has had losses; and one who has two gowns, and everything handsome about him. Bring him away. Oh, if only I'd been written down as an ass!
If you go on thus, you will kill yourself / And 'tis not wisdom thus to second grief / Against yourself.
If you carry on like this, you'll kill yourself; and it isn't wise to help grief attack you like this.

I pray thee, cease thy counsel, / Which falls into mine ears as profitless / As water in a sieve: give not me counsel; / Nor let no comforter delight mine ear / But such a one whose wrongs do suit with mine: / Bring me a father that so lov'd his child, / Whose joy of her is overwhelm'd like mine, / And bid him speak to me of patience; / Measure his woe the length and breadth of mine, / And let it answer every strain for strain, / As thus for thus and such a grief for such, / In every lineament, branch, shape, and form: / If such a one will smile, and stroke his beard; / Bid sorrow wag, cry 'hem' when he should groan, / Patch grief with proverbs; make misfortune drunk / With candle-wasters; bring him yet to me, / And I of him will gather patience. / But there is no such man; for, brother, men / Can counsel and speak comfort to that grief / Which they themselves not feel; but, tasting it, / Their counsel turns to passion, which before / Would give preceptial medicine to rage, / Fetter strong madness in a silken thread, / Charm ache with air and agony with words. / No, no; 'tis all men's office to speak patience / To those that wring under the load of sorrow, / But no man's virtue nor sufficiency / To be so moral when he shall endure / The like himself. Therefore give me no counsel: / My griefs cry louder than advertisement.

Please stop your advice, which falls into my ears as uselessly as water into a sieve. Don't give me advice, and don't let any comforter please my ear except one whose wrongs match mine. Bring me a father who loved his child as much, whose joy in her has been crushed like mine, and tell him to speak to me of patience. Measure his sorrow against the length and breadth of mine, and let it match it pang for pang, this for this and grief for grief, in every feature, branch, shape and form. If a man like that can smile and stroke his beard, tell sorrow to be off, say 'ahem' when he ought to groan, patch up his grief with proverbs and drown his misfortune with late-night philosophers, then bring him to me, and I'll learn patience from him. But there is no such man. For, brother, men can advise and comfort a grief they don't feel themselves; but once they taste it, their advice turns into the same passion that they once wanted to cure with wise sayings, as if they could chain raging madness with a silk thread, charm away pain with breath and agony with words. No, no. It's everyone's job to preach patience to those who writhe under the weight of sorrow, but no one has the strength or the ability to be so moral when he has to endure the same himself. So give me no advice. My griefs cry louder than your warnings.
Therein do men from children nothing differ.
In that, men are no different from children.

I pray thee peace! I will be flesh and blood; / For there was never yet philosopher / That could endure the toothache patiently, / However they have writ the style of gods / And made a push at chance and sufferance.
Please, be quiet! I'll be flesh and blood; for there was never yet a philosopher who could bear toothache patiently, however much they've written like gods and scorned bad luck and suffering.
Yet bend not all the harm upon yourself; / Make those that do offend you suffer too.
Still, don't turn all the harm on yourself. Make those who have wronged you suffer too.
There thou speak'st reason: nay, I will do so. / My soul doth tell me Hero is belied; / And that shall Claudio know; so shall the prince, / And all of them that thus dishonour her.
Now you're talking sense. Yes, I'll do that. My soul tells me Hero has been lied about, and Claudio will know it; so will the prince, and all of them who have dishonoured her like this.
Here comes the prince and Claudio hastily.
Here come the prince and Claudio in a hurry.
Good day to both of you.
Some haste, my lord! well, fare you well, my lord: / Are you so hasty now?—well, all is one.
In a hurry, my lord! Well, goodbye, my lord. Are you in such a hurry now? Well, it doesn't matter.
Nay, do not quarrel with us, good old man.
No, don't quarrel with us, good old man.
If he could right himself with quarrelling, / Some of us would lie low.
If he could put things right by quarrelling, some of us would be lying dead.
Marry, thou dost wrong me; thou dissembler, thou. / Nay, never lay thy hand upon thy sword; I fear thee not.
Why, you are wronging me, you liar, you! No, don't put your hand on your sword; I'm not afraid of you.
Marry, beshrew my hand, / If it should give your age such cause of fear. / In faith, my hand meant nothing to my sword.
Curse my hand if it gave your old age any reason to be afraid. Honestly, my hand meant nothing by touching my sword.

Tush, tush, man! never fleer and jest at me: / I speak not like a dotard nor a fool, / As, under privilege of age, to brag / What I have done being young, or what would do, / Were I not old. Know, Claudio, to thy head, / Thou hast so wrong'd mine innocent child and me / That I am forc'd to lay my reverence by, / And, with grey hairs and bruise of many days, / Do challenge thee to trial of a man. / I say thou hast belied mine innocent child: / Thy slander hath gone through and through her heart, / And she lied buried with her ancestors; / O! in a tomb where never scandal slept, / Save this of hers, fram'd by thy villany!

Come, come, man! Don't sneer and joke at me. I'm not speaking like a senile old man or a fool, who uses his age as an excuse to boast about what he did when he was young, or what he'd do if he weren't old. Know this, Claudio, to your face: you have so wronged my innocent child and me that I'm forced to put aside my dignity and, with my grey hair and the bruises of many years, challenge you to a duel, man to man. I say you have lied about my innocent child. Your slander has gone right through her heart, and she lies buried with her ancestors; oh, in a tomb where scandal never lay before, except this one about her, invented by your villainy!
You say not right, old man,
My lord, my lord, / I'll prove it on his body, if he dare, / Despite his nice fence and his active practice, / His May of youth and bloom of lustihood.
My lord, my lord, I'll prove it on his body, if he dares, despite his fancy swordsmanship and his constant practice, his youth and his strength in its prime.
Away! I will not have to do with you.
Go away! I won't have anything to do with you.
Canst thou so daff me? Thou hast kill'd my child; / If thou kill'st me, boy, thou shalt kill a man.
Can you brush me off like that? You've killed my child. If you kill me, boy, you'll kill a man.

He shall kill two of us, and men indeed: / But that's no matter; let him kill one first: / Win me and wear me; let him answer me. / Come, follow me, boy; come, sir boy, come, follow me. / Sir boy, I'll whip you from your foining fence; / Nay, as I am a gentleman, I will.

He'll have to kill two of us, and real men too. But that doesn't matter; let him kill one first. Beat me and you can have me; let him answer to me. Come, follow me, boy. Come, sir boy, come, follow me. Sir boy, I'll whip you out of your fancy fencing tricks. Yes, as I'm a gentleman, I will.

Content yourself. God knows I lov'd my niece; / And she is dead, slander'd to death by villains, / That dare as well answer a man indeed / As I dare take a serpent by the tongue. / Boys, apes, braggarts, Jacks, milksops!

Calm down. God knows I loved my niece, and she's dead, slandered to death by villains who'd no more dare face a real man than I'd dare grab a snake by its tongue. Boys, apes, braggarts, rascals, milksops!

Hold your content. What, man! I know them, yea, / And what they weigh, even to the utmost scruple, / Scambling, out-facing, fashion-monging boys, / That lie and cog and flout, deprave and slander, / Go antickly, show outward hideousness, / And speak off half a dozen dangerous words, / How they might hurt their enemies, if they durst; / And this is all!

Be quiet. What, man! I know them, yes, and exactly what they're worth, down to the last ounce. Brawling, bullying, fashion-mad boys, who lie and cheat and mock, insult and slander, dress up like clowns, put on a fierce look and spout half a dozen threatening words about how they'd hurt their enemies if they dared; and that's all they are!
Come, 'tis no matter: / Do not you meddle, let me deal in this.
Come, it doesn't matter. Don't you interfere; let me deal with this.
Gentlemen both, we will not wake your patience. / My heart is sorry for your daughter's death; / But, on my honour, she was charg'd with nothing / But what was true and very full of proof.
Gentlemen, we won't try your patience any further. I'm sorry with all my heart for your daughter's death; but, on my honour, she was accused of nothing that wasn't true and fully proved.
No? Come, brother, away. I will be heard.—
No? Come, brother, let's go. I will be heard.—
And shall, or some of us will smart for it.
And you will, or some of us will suffer for it.
See, see; here comes the man we went to seek.
Look, look, here comes the man we went to find.
Welcome, signior: you are almost come to part almost a fray.
Welcome, signior. You've almost arrived in time to break up almost a fight.
We had like to have had our two noses snapped off with two old / men without teeth.
We nearly had our two noses bitten off by two old men without any teeth.
Leonato and his brother. What think'st thou? Had we fought, I / doubt we should have been too young for them.
Leonato and his brother. What do you think? If we'd fought, I suspect we'd have been too young for them.
In a false quarrel there is no true valour. I came to seek you / both.
There's no real courage in an unjust quarrel. I came to find you both.
We have been up and down to seek thee; for we are high-proof / melancholy, and would fain have it beaten away. Wilt thou use / thy wit?
We've been looking everywhere for you, because we're terribly depressed and would love to have it chased away. Will you use your wit?
It is in my scabbard; shall I draw it?
It's in my scabbard. Shall I draw it?
Dost thou wear thy wit by thy side?
Do you wear your wit at your side?
Never any did so, though very many have been beside their wit. I / will bid thee draw, as we do the minstrels; draw, to pleasure us.
No one ever did that, though plenty have been beside themselves. I'll ask you to draw, the way we ask musicians to draw their bows: draw, to entertain us.
As I am an honest man, he looks pale. Art thou sick, or angry?
As I'm an honest man, he looks pale. Are you ill, or angry?
What, courage, man! What though care killed a cat, thou hast / mettle enough in thee to kill care.
What, cheer up, man! Even though worry killed the cat, you've got enough spirit in you to kill worry.
Sir, I shall meet your wit in the career, an you charge it / against me. I pray you choose another subject.
Sir, I'll meet your wit head on, like a jousting knight, if you charge it at me. Please choose another subject.
Nay then, give him another staff: this last was broke cross.
No, then, give him another lance; that last one broke sideways.
By this light, he changes more and more: I think he be angry / indeed.
By this light, he's changing colour more and more. I think he really is angry.
If he be, he knows how to turn his girdle.
If he is, he knows what to do about it: he can turn his belt round and get his sword ready.
Shall I speak a word in your ear?
May I have a word in your ear?
God bless me from a challenge!
God save me from a challenge!

[Aside to CLAUDIO.] / You are a villain, I jest not: I will make it good how you dare, / with what you dare, and when you dare. Do me right, or I will protest / your cowardice. You have killed a sweet lady, and her death shall / fall heavy on you. Let me hear from you.

You're a villain; I'm not joking. I'll prove it however you dare, with whatever weapon you dare, and whenever you dare. Give me satisfaction, or I'll declare you a coward. You've killed a sweet lady, and her death will fall heavily on you. Let me hear from you.
Well I will meet you, so I may have good cheer.
Well, I'll meet you, as long as I get a good meal out of it.
I' faith, I thank him; he hath bid me to a calf's-head and a capon, / the which if I do not carve most curiously, say my knife's naught. / Shall I not find a woodcock too?
Yes, really, I thank him. He has invited me to a calf's head and a castrated cockerel, and if I don't carve them very skilfully, say my knife's no good. Won't I find a woodcock, a stupid bird, too?
Sir, your wit ambles well; it goes easily.
Sir, your wit trots along nicely; it moves at an easy pace.

I'll tell thee how Beatrice praised thy wit the other day. I said, / thou hadst a fine wit. 'True,' says she, 'a fine little one.' / 'No,' said I, 'a great wit.' / 'Right,' said she, 'a great gross one.' / 'Nay,' said I, 'a good wit.' / 'Just,' said she, 'it hurts nobody.' / 'Nay,' said I, 'the gentleman is wise.' / 'Certain,' said she, a wise gentleman.' / 'Nay,' said I, 'he hath the tongues.' / 'That I believe' said she, 'for he swore a thing to me on Monday / night, which he forswore on Tuesday morning: there's a double tongue; / there's two tongues.' / Thus did she, an hour together, trans-shape thy particular virtues; / yet at last she concluded with a sigh, thou wast the properest man in / Italy.

I'll tell you how Beatrice praised your wit the other day. I said you had a fine wit. 'True,' she said, 'a fine little one.' 'No,' I said, 'a great wit.' 'Right,' she said, 'a great fat one.' 'No,' I said, 'a good wit.' 'Exactly,' she said, 'it doesn't hurt anybody.' 'No,' I said, 'the gentleman is wise.' 'Certainly,' she said, 'a wise gentleman.' 'No,' I said, 'he speaks several languages.' 'That I believe,' she said, 'for he swore something to me on Monday night and took it back on Tuesday morning: there's a double tongue, there's two tongues.' Like that, for a whole hour, she twisted every one of your virtues out of shape; and yet at last she concluded, with a sigh, that you were the most handsome man in Italy.
For the which she wept heartily and said she cared not.
And for that she cried her heart out and said she didn't care.
Yea, that she did; but yet, for all that, an if she did not hate him / deadly, she would love him dearly. The old man's daughter told us all.
Yes, she did. But all the same, if she didn't hate him to death, she would love him dearly. The old man's daughter told us everything.
All, all; and moreover, God saw him when he was hid in the garden.
Everything, everything; and what's more, God saw him when he was hiding in the garden, like Adam.
But when shall we set the savage bull's horns on the sensible / Benedick's head?
But when shall we put the wild bull's horns on the sensible Benedick's head?
Yea, and text underneath, 'Here dwells Benedick the married man!'
Yes, with the words underneath: 'Here lives Benedick the married man!'

Fare you well, boy: you know my mind. I will leave you now to your / gossip-like humour; you break jests as braggarts do their blades, / which, God be thanked, hurt not. My lord, for your many courtesies I / thank you: I must discontinue your company. / Your brother the bastard is fled from Messina: you have, among you, / killed a sweet and innocent lady. For my Lord Lack-beard there, he and / I shall meet; and till then, peace be with him.

Goodbye, boy. You know what I mean. I'll leave you now to your gossiping mood. You crack jokes the way braggarts break swords, which, thank God, hurt nobody. My lord, I thank you for your many kindnesses, but I must leave your company. Your brother the bastard has fled from Messina. Between you, you have killed a sweet and innocent lady. As for my Lord No-beard there, he and I will meet; and until then, peace be with him.
In most profound earnest; and, I'll warrant you, for the love of / Beatrice.
Deadly serious; and, I promise you, it's for the love of Beatrice.
What a pretty thing man is when he goes in his doublet and hose / and leaves off his wit!
What a fine thing a man is when he goes out in his jacket and trousers and leaves his brains behind!
He is then a giant to an ape; but then is an ape a doctor to such / a man.
Then he's a giant to an ape; but then an ape is a learned doctor compared with such a man.
But, soft you; let me be: pluck up, my heart, and be sad! Did he / not say my brother was fled?
But wait, let me think. Rouse yourself, my heart, and be serious! Didn't he say my brother had fled?
Come you, sir: if justice cannot tame you, she shall ne'er weigh more / reasons in her balance. Nay, an you be a cursing hypocrite once, you / must be looked to.
Come along, sir. If justice can't tame you, she'll never weigh any more reasons in her scales. No, if you're once a cursing hypocrite, you must be watched.
How now! two of my brother's men bound! Borachio, one!
What's this! Two of my brother's men tied up! Borachio is one of them!
Hearken after their offence, my lord.
Ask what they've done, my lord.
Officers, what offence have these men done?
Officers, what crime have these men committed?

Marry, sir, they have committed false report; moreover, they have / spoken untruths; secondarily, they are slanders; sixth and lastly, / they have belied a lady; thirdly, they have verified unjust things; / and to conclude, they are lying knaves.

Why, sir, they have committed false report; moreover, they have spoken untruths; secondarily, they are slanders; sixth and lastly, they have lied about a lady; thirdly, they have verified unjust things; and to conclude, they are lying villains.
First, I ask thee what they have done; thirdly, I ask thee what's / their offence; sixth and lastly, why they are committed; and, to / conclude, what you lay to their charge?
First, I ask you what they've done; thirdly, I ask you what their crime is; sixth and lastly, why they've been arrested; and to conclude, what are you charging them with?
Rightly reasoned, and in his own division; and, by my troth, there's / one meaning well suited.
Well argued, and in his own order; and upon my word, there's one meaning dressed up in several suits.
Who have you offended, masters, that you are thus bound to your / answer? this learned constable is too cunning to be understood. / What's your offence?
Whom have you offended, gentlemen, that you're tied up to answer for it? This learned constable is too clever to be understood. What's your crime?

Sweet prince, let me go no further to mine answer: do you hear me, and / let this count kill me. I have deceived even your very eyes: what your / wisdoms could not discover, these shallow fools have brought to light; / who, in the night overheard me confessing to this man how Don John / your brother incensed me to slander the Lady Hero; how you were / brought into the orchard and saw me court Margaret in Hero's garments; / how you disgraced her, when you should marry her. / My villany they have upon record; which I had rather seal with my / death than repeat over to my shame. The lady is dead upon mine and my / master's false accusation; and, briefly, I desire nothing but the / reward of a villain.

Sweet prince, let me go no further before answering. Listen to me, and let this count kill me. I have deceived your very eyes. What your wisdom couldn't discover, these simple fools have brought to light. They overheard me in the night confessing to this man how Don John your brother urged me on to slander the Lady Hero; how you were brought into the orchard and saw me court Margaret dressed in Hero's clothes; how you disgraced her when you should have married her. They have recorded my villainy, which I'd rather seal with my death than repeat to my shame. The lady is dead because of my false accusation and my master's; and, in short, I want nothing but a villain's reward.
Runs not this speech like iron through your blood?
Doesn't this speech run through your blood like iron?
I have drunk poison whiles he utter'd it.
I've drunk poison while he spoke it.
But did my brother set thee on to this?
But did my brother put you up to this?
Yea; and paid me richly for the practice of it.
Yes, and paid me richly for doing it.
He is compos'd and fram'd of treachery: / And fled he is upon this villany.
He's made and shaped entirely out of treachery, and he has fled because of this villainy.
Sweet Hero! now thy image doth appear In the rare semblance that / I lov'd it first.
Sweet Hero! Now your image appears in the rare beauty I loved at first.
Come, bring away the plaintiffs: by this time our sexton hath / reformed Signior Leonato of the matter. And masters, do not forget / to specify, when time and place shall serve, that I am an ass.

Come, bring away the plaintiffs (he means defendants). By now our clerk has reformed (informed) Signior Leonato about the matter. And gentlemen, don't forget to state, when the time and place are right, that I am an ass.
Here, here comes Master Signior Leonato, and the sexton too.
Here, here comes Master Signior Leonato, and the clerk too.
Which is the villain? Let me see his eyes, / That, when I note another man like him, / I may avoid him. Which of these is he?
Which is the villain? Let me see his eyes, so that when I notice another man like him, I can avoid him. Which of these is he?
If you would know your wronger, look on me.
If you want to know who wronged you, look at me.
Art thou the slave that with thy breath hast kill'd / Mine innocent child?
Are you the wretch who killed my innocent child with your breath?

No, not so, villain; thou beliest thyself: / Here stand a pair of honourable men; / A third is fled, that had a hand in it. / I thank you, princes, for my daughter's death: / Record it with your high and worthy deeds. / 'Twas bravely done, if you bethink you of it.

No, not so, villain; you're lying about yourself. Here stand a pair of honourable men; a third, who had a hand in it, has fled. I thank you, princes, for my daughter's death. Record it with your noble and worthy deeds. It was bravely done, if you think about it.
I know not how to pray your patience; / Yet I must speak. Choose your revenge yourself; / Impose me to what penance your invention / Can lay upon my sin: yet sinn'd I not / But in mistaking.
I don't know how to ask for your patience, yet I must speak. Choose your revenge yourself. Give me whatever penance you can think of for my sin; and yet I didn't sin, except by being mistaken.
By my soul, nor I: / And yet, to satisfy this good old man, / I would bend under any heavy weight / That he'll enjoin me to.
On my soul, nor did I. And yet, to satisfy this good old man, I'd bend under any heavy burden he orders me to carry.

I cannot bid you bid my daughter live; / That were impossible; but, I pray you both, / Possess the people in Messina here / How innocent she died; and if your love / Can labour aught in sad invention, / Hang her an epitaph upon her tomb, / And sing it to her bones: sing it to-night. / To-morrow morning come you to my house, / And since you could not be my son-in-law, / Be yet my nephew. My brother hath a daughter, / Almost the copy of my child that's dead, / And she alone is heir to both of us: / Give her the right you should have given her cousin, / And so dies my revenge.

I can't order you to tell my daughter to live; that would be impossible. But I beg you both, let the people here in Messina know how innocent she was when she died. And if your love can produce anything in a sad poem, hang an epitaph on her tomb and sing it to her bones; sing it tonight. Tomorrow morning come to my house, and since you couldn't be my son-in-law, be my nephew instead. My brother has a daughter who is almost a copy of my child who's dead, and she alone is heir to both of us. Give her the rights you should have given her cousin, and so my revenge dies.
O noble sir, / Your over-kindness doth wring tears from me! / I do embrace your offer; and dispose / For henceforth of poor Claudio.
Oh, noble sir, your great kindness wrings tears from me! I accept your offer, and from now on poor Claudio is yours to command.

To-morrow then I will expect your coming; / To-night I take my leave. This naughty man / Shall face to face be brought to Margaret, / Who, I believe, was pack'd in all this wrong, / Hir'd to it by your brother.
Then I'll expect you tomorrow. Tonight I'll say goodbye. This wicked man will be brought face to face with Margaret, who I believe was in on all this wrong, hired to do it by your brother.
No, by my soul she was not; / Nor knew not what she did when she spoke to me; / But always hath been just and virtuous / In anything that I do know by her.
No, on my soul, she wasn't. She didn't know what she was doing when she spoke to me, and she has always been honest and good in everything I know of her.

Moreover, sir,—which, indeed, is not under white and black,— this / plaintiff here, the offender, did call me ass: I beseech you, let it / be remembered in his punishment. / And also, the watch heard them talk of one Deformed: they say he wears / a key in his ear and a lock hanging by it, and borrows money in God's / name, the which he hath used so long and never paid, that now men grow / hard-hearted, and will lend nothing for God's sake. Pray you, examine / him upon that point.

Moreover, sir, which indeed isn't written down in black and white, this plaintiff here, the offender, called me an ass. I beg you, let it be remembered in his punishment. And also, the watch heard them talk of one Deformed. They say he wears a key in his ear and a lock hanging by it, and borrows money in God's name, which he has done for so long without ever paying it back that men are growing hard-hearted and won't lend anything for God's sake. Please question him on that point.
I thank thee for thy care and honest pains.
Thank you for your care and honest efforts.
Your worship speaks like a most thankful and reverent youth, and / I praise God for you.
Your worship speaks like a most thankful and respectful youth, and I praise God for you.
God save the foundation! (He thanks him as if he were a charity.)
Go, I discharge thee of thy prisoner, and I thank thee.
Go. I release you from your prisoner, and I thank you.

I leave an arrant knave with your worship; which I beseech your / worship to correct yourself, for the example of others. God keep / your worship! I wish your worship well; God restore you to health! / I humbly give you leave to depart, and if a merry meeting may be / wished, God prohibit it! Come, neighbour.

I leave a complete villain with your worship, whom I beg your worship to correct yourself, as an example to others. God keep your worship! I wish your worship well; God restore you to health! I humbly give you permission to leave; and if a happy meeting may be wished for, God prohibit (he means permit) it! Come, neighbour.
Farewell, my lords: we look for you to-morrow.
Goodbye, my lords. We expect you tomorrow.
[To the Watch.] Bring you these fellows on. We'll talk with / Margaret, How her acquaintance grew with this lewd fellow.
Bring these fellows along. We'll talk with Margaret about how she came to know this wicked fellow.
Pray thee, sweet Mistress Margaret, deserve well at my hands by / helping me to the speech of Beatrice.
Please, sweet Mistress Margaret, earn my gratitude by helping me to speak with Beatrice.
Will you then write me a sonnet in praise of my beauty?
Will you write me a sonnet praising my beauty, then?
In so high a style, Margaret, that no man living shall come over / it; for, in most comely truth, thou deservest it.
In such a high style, Margaret, that no living man will come over it, for in all honest truth, you deserve it.
To have no man come over me! why, shall I always keep below stairs?
No man come over me! Why, am I always to stay downstairs with the servants?
Thy wit is as quick as the greyhound's mouth; it catches.
Your wit is as quick as a greyhound's mouth: it catches.
And yours as blunt as the fencer's foils, which hit, but hurt not.
And yours is as blunt as a fencer's practice swords, which hit but don't hurt.
A most manly wit, Margaret; it will not hurt a woman: and so, I / pray thee, call Beatrice. I give thee the bucklers.
A very manly wit, Margaret: it won't hurt a woman. And so, please, call Beatrice. I surrender; I give you the shields.
Give us the swords, we have bucklers of our own.
Give us the swords. We have shields of our own.
If you use them, Margaret, you must put in the pikes with a vice; / and they are dangerous weapons for maids.
If you use them, Margaret, you must screw in the spikes with a vice; and they're dangerous weapons for virgins.
Well, I will call Beatrice to you, who I think hath legs.
Well, I'll call Beatrice for you, who I think has legs.

The god of love, ~That sits above, And knows me, and knows me, ~How / pitiful I deserve,— I mean, in singing: but in loving, Leander the / good swimmer, Troilus the first employer of panders, and a whole book / full of these quondam carpet-mongers, whose names yet run smoothly in / the even road of a blank verse, why, they were never so truly turned / over and over as my poor self in love. / Marry, I cannot show it in rime; I have tried: I can find out no rime / to 'lady' but 'baby', an innocent rhyme; for 'scorn,' 'horn', a hard / rime; for 'school', 'fool', a babbling rhyme; very ominous endings: / no, I was not born under a riming planet, nor I cannot woo in festival / terms.

'The god of love, who sits above, and knows me, and knows me, how pitiful I deserve...' I mean at singing. But at loving: Leander the good swimmer, Troilus the first man to use a go-between, and a whole book full of these old-time ladies' men, whose names still run smoothly along the even road of blank verse, why, they were never so truly turned head over heels as my poor self in love. But I can't show it in rhyme. I've tried. I can't find a rhyme for 'lady' except 'baby', a childish rhyme; for 'scorn', 'horn', a harsh rhyme; for 'school', 'fool', a silly rhyme. Very unlucky endings. No, I wasn't born under a rhyming planet, and I can't woo in fancy holiday language.
Sweet Beatrice, wouldst thou come when I called thee?
Sweet Beatrice, would you come when I called you?
Yea, signior; and depart when you bid me.
Yes, signior, and leave when you tell me to.
'Then' is spoken; fare you well now: and yet, ere I go, let me go with / that I came for; which is, with knowing what hath passed between you / and Claudio.
'Then' has been said, so goodbye now. And yet before I go, let me go with what I came for, which is knowing what has passed between you and Claudio.
Only foul words; and thereupon I will kiss thee.
Only foul words; and for that I'll kiss you.
Foul words is but foul wind, and foul wind is but foul breath, and / foul breath is noisome; therefore I will depart unkissed.
Foul words are only foul wind, and foul wind is only foul breath, and foul breath is disgusting, so I'll leave unkissed.

Thou hast frighted the word out of his right sense, so forcible is thy / wit. But I must tell thee plainly, Claudio undergoes my challenge, and / either I must shortly hear from him, or I will subscribe him a coward. / And, I pray thee now, tell me, for which of my bad parts didst thou / first fall in love with me?

You've frightened the word out of its proper meaning, your wit is so forceful. But I must tell you plainly: Claudio has received my challenge, and either I'll hear from him soon or I'll publicly declare him a coward. And now, please tell me, for which of my bad qualities did you first fall in love with me?

For them all together; which maintained so politic a state of evil / that they will not admit any good part to intermingle with them. / But for which of my good parts did you first suffer love for me?
For all of them together, which run such a well-organised state of evil that they won't let any good quality mix with them. But for which of my good qualities did you first suffer love for me?
'Suffer love,' a good epithet! I do suffer love indeed, for I love / thee against my will.
'Suffer love': a good phrase! I do suffer love indeed, because I love you against my will.
In spite of your heart, I think. Alas, poor heart! If you spite it / for my sake, I will spite it for yours; for I will never love that / which my friend hates.
In spite of your heart, I think. Ah, poor heart! If you spite it for my sake, I'll spite it for yours; because I'll never love something my friend hates.
Thou and I are too wise to woo peaceably.
You and I are too clever to woo peacefully.
It appears not in this confession: there's not one wise man among / twenty that will praise himself.
That doesn't show in this confession. Not one wise man in twenty will praise himself.

An old, an old instance, Beatrice, that lived in the time of good / neighbours. If a man do not erect in this age his own tomb ere he / dies, he shall live no longer in monument than the bell rings and / the widow weeps.

An old, old saying, Beatrice, from the days of good neighbours who praised each other. In this age, if a man doesn't put up his own monument before he dies, he'll be remembered no longer than the funeral bell rings and the widow weeps.
And how long is that think you?
And how long is that, do you think?

Question: why, an hour in clamour and a quarter in rheum: therefore is / it most expedient for the wise,—if Don Worm, his conscience, find no / impediment to the contrary,—to be the trumpet of his own virtues, as / I am to myself. So much for praising myself, who, I myself will bear / witness, is praiseworthy. And now tell me, how doth your cousin?

Good question. Why, an hour of bell-ringing and a quarter of an hour of tears. So it's best for the wise man, if Sir Worm, his conscience, has no objection, to blow the trumpet for his own virtues, as I do for myself. So much for praising myself, and I myself will testify that I'm praiseworthy. And now tell me, how is your cousin?
Serve God, love me, and mend. There will I leave you too, for here / comes one in haste.
Serve God, love me, and get better. I'll leave you there too, because here comes someone in a hurry.

Madam, you must come to your uncle. Yonder's old coil at home: it is / proved, my Lady Hero hath been falsely accused, the prince and Claudio / mightily abused; and Don John is the author of all, who is fled and / gone. Will you come presently?

Madam, you must come to your uncle. There's a great commotion at home. It's been proved that my Lady Hero was falsely accused, the prince and Claudio badly deceived, and Don John is behind it all, and he has fled. Will you come at once?
Will you go hear this news, signior?
Will you come and hear this news, signior?
I will live in thy heart, die in thy lap, and be buried in thy eyes; / and moreover I will go with thee to thy uncle's.
I'll live in your heart, die in your lap and be buried in your eyes; and what's more, I'll go with you to your uncle's.
Is this the monument of Leonato?

[Reads from a scroll.] / Done to death by slanderous tongues / Was the Hero that here lies: / Death, in guerdon of her wrongs, / Gives her fame which never dies. / So the life that died with shame / Lives in death with glorious fame. / Hang thou there upon the tomb, / Praising her when I am dumb. / Now, music, sound, and sing your solemn hymn.

'Done to death by slandering tongues was the Hero who lies here. Death, as a reward for her wrongs, gives her fame that never dies. So the life that died in shame lives on in death with glorious fame.' Hang there on the tomb, praising her when I am silent. Now, music, play and sing your solemn hymn.

Pardon, goddess of the night, / Those that slew thy virgin knight; / For the which, with songs of woe, / Round about her tomb they go. / Midnight, assist our moan; / Help us to sigh and groan, / Heavily, heavily: / Graves, yawn and yield your dead, / Till death be uttered, / Heavily, heavily.

Forgive, goddess of the night, those who killed your virgin follower; for which, with songs of sorrow, they walk around her tomb. Midnight, help our mourning; help us to sigh and groan, heavily, heavily. Graves, open and give up your dead, until death is fully spoken of, heavily, heavily.
Now, unto thy bones good night! / Yearly will I do this rite.
Now, good night to your bones! I'll perform this ritual every year.

Good morrow, masters: put your torches out. / The wolves have prey'd; and look, the gentle day, / Before the wheels of Phoebus, round about / Dapples the drowsy east with spots of grey. / Thanks to you all, and leave us: fare you well.

Good morning, gentlemen. Put your torches out. The wolves have finished hunting; and look, the gentle dawn, ahead of the sun god's chariot, is dappling the sleepy east with spots of grey. Thank you all, and leave us. Goodbye.
Good morrow, masters: each his several way.
Good morning, gentlemen. Each go your own way.
Come, let us hence, and put on other weeds; And then to Leonato's / we will go.
Come, let's go and change our clothes, and then we'll go to Leonato's.
And Hymen now with luckier issue speed's, / Than this for whom we rend'red up this woe!
And may Hymen, god of marriage, bring us a happier outcome than the one for whom we've performed this mourning!
Did I not tell you she was innocent?
Didn't I tell you she was innocent?

So are the prince and Claudio, who accus'd her / Upon the error that you heard debated: / But Margaret was in some fault for this, / Although against her will, as it appears / In the true course of all the question.

So are the prince and Claudio, who accused her because of the mistake you heard discussed. But Margaret was partly to blame for this, although it was against her will, as appears from the whole investigation.
Well, I am glad that all things sort so well.
Well, I'm glad everything has turned out so well.
And so am I, being else by faith enforc'd / To call young Claudio to a reckoning for it.
And so am I, since otherwise I'd be bound by my promise to call young Claudio to account for it.
Well, daughter, and you gentlewomen all, / Withdraw into a chamber by yourselves, / And when I send for you, come hither mask'd: / The prince and Claudio promis'd by this hour / To visit me.
Well, daughter, and all you ladies, go into a room by yourselves, and when I send for you, come here masked. The prince and Claudio promised to visit me at this hour.
You know your office, brother; / You must be father to your brother's daughter, / And give her to young Claudio.
You know your part, brother. You must act as father to your brother's daughter and give her to young Claudio.
Which I will do with confirm'd countenance.
Which I'll do with a straight face.
Friar, I must entreat your pains, I think.
Friar, I think I must ask for your help.
To bind me, or undo me; one of them. / Signior Leonato, truth it is, good signior, / Your niece regards me with an eye of favour.
To bind me or undo me, one or the other. Signior Leonato, the truth is, good signior, your niece looks at me with favour.
That eye my daughter lent her: 'tis most true.
That eye was lent to her by my daughter; that's very true.
And I do with an eye of love requite her.
And I return her love with a loving eye.
The sight whereof I think, you had from me, / From Claudio, and the prince. But what's your will?
I think you got that view of her from me, from Claudio and from the prince. But what is it you want?

Your answer, sir, is enigmatical: / But, for my will, my will is your good will / May stand with ours, this day to be conjoin'd / In the state of honourable marriage: / In which, good friar, I shall desire your help.

Your answer, sir, is a riddle. But as for what I want, I want your goodwill to agree with ours, so that we can be joined today in the state of honourable marriage; and for that, good friar, I'll need your help.
My heart is with your liking.
My heart agrees with your wishes.
And my help. Here comes the prince and Claudio.
And my help with them. Here come the prince and Claudio.
Good morrow to this fair assembly.
Good morning to this fine company.
Good morrow, prince; good morrow, Claudio: / We here attend you. Are you yet determin'd / To-day to marry with my brother's daughter?
Good morning, prince; good morning, Claudio. We're waiting for you here. Are you still determined to marry my brother's daughter today?
I'll hold my mind, were she an Ethiope.
I'll stick to my decision even if she were an Ethiopian.
Call her forth, brother: here's the friar ready.
Call her in, brother. The friar is ready.
Good morrow, Benedick. Why, what's the matter, / That you have such a February face, / So full of frost, of storm and cloudiness?
Good morning, Benedick. Why, what's the matter, that you have such a February face, so full of frost, storms and clouds?

I think he thinks upon the savage bull. / Tush! fear not, man, we'll tip thy horns with gold, / And all Europa shall rejoice at thee, / As once Europa did at lusty Jove, / When he would play the noble beast in love.

I think he's thinking about the wild bull. Come on, don't be afraid, man; we'll tip your horns with gold, and all Europe will delight in you, as Europa once delighted in lusty Jove when he played the noble bull in love.
Bull Jove, sir, had an amiable low: / And some such strange bull leap'd your father's cow, / And got a calf in that same noble feat, / Much like to you, for you have just his bleat.
Jove the bull, sir, had a lovely moo; and some strange bull like that jumped on your father's cow and fathered a calf in that same noble act, very much like you, because you have exactly his bleat.
For this I owe you: here comes other reckonings.
I'll pay you back for this. Here come other matters to settle.
Which is the lady I must seize upon?
Which is the lady I must take?
This same is she, and I do give you her.
This is the one, and I give her to you.
Why then, she's mine. Sweet, let me see your face.
Why then, she's mine. Sweetheart, let me see your face.
No, that you shall not, till you take her hand / Before this friar, and swear to marry her.
No, you shall not, until you take her hand in front of this friar and swear to marry her.
Give me your hand: before this holy friar, / I am your husband, if you like of me.
Give me your hand. In front of this holy friar, I am your husband, if you'll have me.
And when I liv'd, I was your other wife: / [Unmasking.] And when you lov'd, you were my other husband.
And when I was alive, I was your other wife; and when you loved me, you were my other husband.

I'll tell you what, prince: a whole university of wisecrackers couldn't mock me out of my good mood. Do you think I care about a satire or a witty poem? No. If a man is going to be beaten down by clever remarks, he won't dare wear anything fine about him. In short, since I intend to marry, I'll take no notice of anything the world can say against it. So never mock me for what I've said against marriage, because man is a fickle creature, and that's my conclusion. As for you, Claudio, I was planning to beat you; but since you're going to be my relative, live unbruised, and love my cousin.

Come, come, we're friends. Let's have a dance before we're married, to lighten our own hearts and our wives' feet.
